#6200. Aeromexico 787s Get Makeover With New Business Class, Premium Economy

Aeromexico is planning some major upgrades to its wide body fleet, which consists exclusively of Boeing 787s. This is interesting on many levels — we’ll see the larger Dreamliners get all-new business class cabins plus premium economy for the first time, we’ll see the smaller Dreamliners get the old business class cabins of the bigger Dreamliners, and we’ll see the airline adopt some Delta-style branding.

To start, let me provide the context that Aeromexico’s Boeing 787 fleet currently consists of 25 planes, including:

Aeromexico is planning on fully overhauling the premium cabins on these planes, as was announced by the company’s CEO at this week’s APEX FTE EXPO 2026.

The plan is for the 787-9s to get all-new cabins, and in the process, the 787-8s will get the old business class seats from the 787-9s. That means the 787-8s will get reverse herringbone seats, which are still competitive, but of course not cutting edge (though still a huge improvement over the pairs of seats currently on the planes).

The 787-9s will really become the next-generation flagship planes for the airline, though some patience will be required. The expectation is that the first of these Dreamliners will be retrofitted in the next 18 to 24 months (so hopefully by some point in 2028), and then it’ll likely take a couple of years for the fleet to be upgraded.

We’ll talk more about the new business class product as such in a bit, but the idea is that the 787-9s will get business class suites, including a front row “business class plus” product. On top of that, the 787-9s will be getting a premium economy cabin for the first time.

The plane will also have up to 70% more premium seats than before. Currently, Aeromexico’s 787-9s have 36 business class seats, while the retrofitted planes will have a total of 61 premium seats, between business class and premium economy. So I suspect the business class cabin won’t actually get that much bigger, but instead, most of that premium addition will come in the form of the new premium economy cabin.

It’s also worth mentioning that Aeromexico is adopting some Delta-style branding, as Delta owns a 20% stake in Aeromexico, and the two airlines have a close partnership.

Aeromexico’s new premium products will be known as Premier One Suites Plus (the “business class plus” product), Premier One Suites (business class), and Premier (premium economy). It seems the 787-8 business class will just be branded as Premier One, given the lack of suites with doors. That all sure seems to be inspired by the Delta One branding that’s used by the carrier’s partner.

Seth Miller from PaxEx.Aero flags how Aeromexico’s new Boeing 787-9 business class suite is from Recaro, as the airline is reportedly the launch customer for this new product. However, the exact product hasn’t actually been named.

Aeromexico CEO Dr. Andres Conesa unveiled the carrier's new premium economy cabin plus refreshed business class seat at #APEXFTEExpo in Singapore this week.Full teaser video in the story: paxex.aero/first-look-a….#PaxEx$RTX

I believe this might be an evolution of the Recaro R7 product (LATAM’s newest 787 business class), which in and of itself was already an evolution of the Recaro CL6720 product (Iberia’s newest A350 business class).

It seems that what was unveiled earlier this year was the new Recaro R7 Horizon concept, which is the same idea, but with upgraded technology and customization.

I imagine that we’ll learn more in the coming months, as this was an unusual way to unveil a new product. But this does seem to be officially happening, so it’s something to look forward to… down the road.

Aeromexico is planning some big upgrades to its Dreamliners. The Boeing 787-9s will be getting all-new cabins, including new business class suites, plus a premium economy cabin for the first time. There will even be a premium business product in the first row, with the products marketed as Premier One Suites Plus, Premier One Suites, and Premier.

As this happens, the 787-8s will be getting the old reverse herringbone seats from the 787-9s, so that will be a meaningful upgrade as well. You can expect these new cabins to roll out starting at some point in 2028, so some patience will be required. I can’t wait to learn more!

What do you make of Aeromexico’s Dreamliner plans?

#6199. Hah: Emirates Puts Auditors On Flights To “Provide Support & Guidance” To Crew

Emirates is known for its incredibly high service standards, and that’s largely thanks to the hierarchical system onboard. You have different ranks of flight attendants, then you have supervisors overseeing business class and economy, and then those supervisors report to the purser.

This system ensures that there’s accountability onboard, and I think that lack of hierarchy is one of the reasons we have service issues at airlines in the US, as no one is really in charge. Anyway, along those lines, Emirates has just introduced a new initiative, which will no doubt be controversial among flight attendants…

Emirates has a rank above pursers, which are the Standard Pursers (which is a weird name, but the idea is that they’re there to audit and enforce “standards”). These are specially trained former pursers who no longer work flights in a standard capacity (at least until now), but instead, they audit the crews onboard flights. They have completely different uniforms.

Emirates’ Chief Operations Officer, Adel Alredha, has just taken to Instagram to highlight a new initiative involving this small group of employees:

On 3 November, Emirates introduced a new initiative on select flights, which will have Standard Pursers work alongside cabin crew teams to provide support and guidance to ensure consistently high standards of service.

This step reflects the airline’s ongoing commitment to maintaining service quality and elevating the customer experience.

So rather than just auditing the cabins, these Emirates employees will actually be working in the cabin, and that’s sure to ruffle some feathers…

A post shared by Adel Alredha (@adelalredha)

Emirates is of course an incredibly global airline with staff from around the world, and I know a thing or two about the internal politics that crews deal with, the different working environments based on who is purser, etc.

For example, you have some pursers who are incredibly strict to the point that they make their colleagues feel uncomfortable and nervous, while you have other pursers who try to encourage good service by creating a fun environment, etc.

It goes without saying that historically when a flight had an auditor onboard, everyone would be on their absolute best behavior. In a way that’s no doubt a bit chaotic and stressful, since they’re worried about repercussions if something goes wrong.

When it comes to this initiative, on the one hand, it’s probably good for these auditors to get some renewed firsthand experience with service, guest expectations, etc. On the other hand, I have to imagine that from the perspective of other crew members, this won’t necessarily be perceived as an effort to “provide support and guidance.”

As one commenter on the Instagram post notes, “this is like sending a child to school along with mama with a stick to correct the kid every step.” Another commenter notes “as if there wasn’t already enough pressure on the crew.”

I am curious if these flights are still staffed with a regular purser in addition to this special rank of purser, because that could also cause a bit of a butting-of-heads. If an auditor is onboard in their official capacity, it’s clear what everyone’s role onboard is (everyone is there to make sure they perform well!). But if the auditor is there to simply “provide support,” that blurs the lines a little bit, no?

Anyway, there aren’t actually that many of these auditor pursers at the airline, so presumably only a small percentage of flights will have them. But if you do notice a crew member with a completely different uniform (more silver in color), now you know what’s going on. That would also be a great person to provide any feedback to, because they actually have the ability to get those details to the right person.

Emirates has Standard Pursers, who are essentially auditors who are assigned select flights, in order to evaluate service from the crew. As of this month, these auditors are also starting to work on flights alongside the crew, to “provide support and guidance.”

There’s no denying that this is an initiative that will make some crew members nervous, since this definitely blurs the line of auditing vs. having an extra set of helping hands. However, given the relatively small number of auditors, they shouldn’t be on too many flights. But if you do see someone in a completely different uniform (other than the standard female purser uniform), then now you know what’s going on.

What do you make of this Emirates initiative?

I am a predominantly ground based cabin crew manager for a large European airline but also work as supernumerary crew on 2-3 long haul flights per year. #6198. Jeffries puts immigration bill high on Democratic priority list

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., holds a news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is signaling Democrats will move quickly on immigration legislation when the party reclaims the House in January, while acknowledging it still has work to do in shaping its healthcare agenda.

Jeffries, who is expected to secure his spot as the next speaker during a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday, identified immigration and health care as among the top priorities for the incoming majority during a Tuesday news conference.

“One of the things that we need to do is to move the Dream and Promise Act for DACA recipients and TPS recipients,” Jeffries said, referring to a Democratic bill introduced last year. “We should actually move that bill immediately.”

The proposal aims to create a path to citizenship for certain Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals recipients and Temporary Protected Status holders. Similar legislation has been a top priority for Democrats in both chambers for more than a decade, with Democrats unable to advance this bill in the House while Republicans have held the majority.

Jeffries also reiterated his calls to rein in Immigration and Customs Enforcement and redirect funding allocated to the agency through Republicans' budget law known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, while expressing a desire for bipartisan cooperation on immigration more broadly.

“We think the border should be safe and strong and secure, and we think our immigration system overall is broken,” Jeffries said. “We need to fix it in a comprehensive way, and certainly, it's our hope that a handful of Republicans will be willing to join us, so we can fix it in a bipartisan way.”

On healthcare, however, Jeffries offered fewer specifics, suggesting Democrats still have decisions to make before taking control of the chamber. Democrats broadly agree on the need to restore subsidies for plans purchased through health insurance markets that expired at the end of 2025. But the question of what additional steps the party should pursue with the goal of expanding coverage and lowering prices is likely to be a major test of Democratic leadership’s ability to find consensus among its robust new majority.

When asked how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that's all part of an ongoing conversation.”

The New York Democrat outlined several broader healthcare priorities, including reversing Medicaid cuts enacted under President Donald Trump, extending Affordable Care Act tax credits, all of which Democrats have vowed to do over the last year.

“Out of the gate, what we clearly have to do is fix our broken healthcare system in terms of the damage that's been done by Donald Trump and MAGA extremists over the last two years, and that clearly involves reversing the Medicaid cuts and extending the Affordable Care Act tax credits, and beginning to engage in supporting medical research, particularly things like research for pediatric cancer,” Jeffries added.

Democrats established a healthcare working group earlier this Congress, led by Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. and Terri Sewell, D-Ala., to gather perspectives and develop policy proposals as the party works toward a broader agenda.

Without an announced challenger, Jeffries has expressed confidence that he’ll secure the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who have said they remain “undecided” ahead of Wednesday’s elections. Jeffries, who was introduced as “Speaker Jeffries” on election night, said last week he was “very confident we’ll get there” and confirmed that the caucus will hold a recorded vote in the contest.

Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to go forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives, many aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America, had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

Jeffries said Tuesday the approach mirrors the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who is best positioned to lead based on “track record, experience and vision.”

This report was corrected to reflect Rep. Nancy Pelosi’s status as a current member.

#6196. Bilt Rent Day Promotion December 2026: JetBlue Mosaic Status Challenge

Bilt is the platform known for providing rewards for housing payments. Earlier this year we saw massive changes at Bilt, including an overhaul of the credit card portfolio, plus new ways that housing rewards are offered.

There are many innovative things about Bilt, including that there’s a Bilt Rent Day promotion on the first day of each month. With a new month being right around the corner, I’d like to cover the details of the December 2026 Bilt Rent Day offer, as it includes both a JetBlue Mosaic elite status challenge, as well as an up to 100% bonus on statement credit redemptions (which isn’t a very good deal). It’s interesting to see a second month in a row with no transfer bonus…

There are a couple of aspects to the Bilt Rent Day promotion, including the ability to earn bonus points (which is the same every month), plus at least one additional promotion.

Note that Bilt Rent Day promotions are generally valid from 12:00AM ET until 11:59PM PT, so technically you have around 27 hours to take advantage of them.

Bilt has a portfolio of credit cards, including the no annual fee Bilt Blue Card (learn more), $95 annual fee Bilt Obsidian Card (learn more), and $495 annual fee Bilt Palladium Card (learn more) (Rates & Fees). Personally, I think the Bilt Palladium Card is by far the most lucrative.

On the first day of each month, you earn double those rewards on these cards, and earn up to 1,000 bonus points each month. It could be worth strategically making some purchases on the first day of each month to maximize this as much as possible.

For example, with double points, the Bilt Palladium Card offers 4x points on everyday spending on the first day of the month, so that’s pretty awesome (up to a cap of $500 worth of spending, since that would earn you 1,000 bonus points).

On December 1, 2026, Bilt is offering a bonus when members redeem points for statement credits. The bonus you’re eligible for depends on which Bilt credit card you have, as follows:

Let me cut to the chase — don’t redeem your points this way. It’s a bad value. Ordinarily you get 0.55 cents per Bilt point for statement credit redemptions, so even with a 100% bonus, you’re looking at getting 1.1 cents per point. Hard pass.

On December 1, 2026, Bilt is offering a JetBlue TrueBlue Mosaic status match challenge, and the status you’re eligible for depends on your Bilt elite status, as follows:

The status is matched for a period of three months, with no additional activity required to maintain it for that period. Then, during those three months, members can extend the status through January 31, 2028, by completing the following requirements:

Regardless of which tier you initially match to, the status you get to keep is based on the activity over the course of those three months. As a reminder, you earn one tile for every $100 spent on JetBlue, or every $1,000 spent on a co-branded JetBlue credit card. So renewing status requires anywhere from $1,000 to $4,000 of airfare spending, or $10,000 to $40,000 of credit card spending.

This of course comes at a generally useful time for JetBlue elite status, given that the airline is introducing first class, with space available upgrades being an elite perk. However, it’s worth emphasizing that this really isn’t such a special offer, as it’s basically just JetBlue’s standard status match challenge offer. Except in this case, you can unlock it with Bilt elite status rather than airline elite status.

On the first day of each month, Bilt offers a Rent Day promotion. In addition to earning up to double points for purchases, for December 2026, there are two offers members can take advantage of.

One offer is for up to a 100% bonus on statement credit redemptions, which can get you at most 1.1 cents per point of value. Please don’t redeem your points that way. JetBlue is also offering a status match challenge, whereby Bilt members can receive Mosaic 1 or Mosaic 2 status for a period of 90 days, and can then extend status through early 2028, with the opportunity to earn up to Mosaic 3 status, based on how many tiles are earned.

#6195. Why Aerolíneas Argentinas Is Basically An Ultra Low Cost Carrier In Disguise

This might seem like a rather niche topic to cover in my first week at OMAAT, but after Ben mentioned this story in his intro article, I thought it made sense to follow up fast with an explainer.

As a flag carrier of the 3rd most populous nation in South America, I went into my Aerolíneas Argentinas flight with them at the start of the year expecting some pretty standard things: enjoying my SkyTeam benefits, lounge access, and, most importantly of all for someone living out of a suitcase, checked bag allowance.

However, I quickly discovered that the airline is basically an ultra-low-cost airline masquerading as a full-service carrier.

I needed to get from Buenos Aires to Mendoza for a friend’s 40th birthday celebrations. Options were pretty limited, with nonstop flights available with either JetSmart or, indeed, Aerolíneas Argentinas. I try to avoid low-cost airlines when possible, because, quite simply, I enjoy the flying experience, and low-cost airlines tend to suck every enjoyable element out of it.

Other pros to booking Aerolíneas Argentinas, personally:

After researching my options, I used Flying Blue miles to book two single tickets from Buenos Aires Jorge Newbery Aeroparque Airport (AEP) to Mendoza’s El Plumerillo Airport (MDZ).

I can’t remember how much the fares were when I was planning the trip, but each one-way flight cost a total of 7,500 miles and less than $10 in taxes and fees.

Looking now at example fares for January next year, round-trips for Aerolíneas’ lowest and most restrictive fare category (more on that to come) start at around $120.

I know it’s not a hard-and-fast rule, but I’ve come to expect that, most of the time, the baggage allowance listed on the booking confirmation is correct. This is often true with redemptions, such as British Airways, which notably offers and acknowledges a 23 kg baggage allowance when redeeming Avios, even for a short-haul flight in economy.

The confirmation email I received clearly noted 1x checked bag with a 23 kg limit.

Again, the attached PDF stated that I’d have 1x checked bag included.

As the Argentinian scamsters would have it, I learned at check-in that the airline has a 15 kg weight limit for checked bags on domestic flights. I tried to plead my case and showed the rather unhelpful check-in agent my booking confirmation, but he basically said, “that means nothing.”

So they weigh your bag, give you a ticket, and then you have to exit the terminal building and find this little cashier where they collect their scammy little earnings. And what better place to proudly display a “SkyTeam Alliance Member” sign at the very desk where the airline also proudly collects baggage fees from SkyTeam elite status holders, even when traveling on award tickets?

Once I’d been charged the fee of around $17, I had to join another queue back inside and show them I’d paid for the extra weight before they’d dispatch my bag. You might look at the $32 in fees I paid and think, “What is he complaining about?” But this isn’t about the actual amount of money; it’s the principle.

Only after the debacle did I learn the extent of Aerolíneas Argentinas’ domestic fare restrictions. Imagine paying $510 (more than four times the cheapest fare) for a “premium economy” ticket and still only getting 15 kg checked baggage allowance, no Fast Pass, no priority boarding (what?), and no lounge access. The latter isn’t such a big deal as Aerolíneas Argentinas doesn’t even have its own lounge at AEP.

Airline loyalty is really important to me, and I generally value it more than the ability to redeem miles. Maybe I’ll get into that another day…

Things got off to a fairly normal start when I saw the Sky Priority check-in kiosks at Aeroparque.

That feeling of normalcy lasted as long as it took me to get from the sign to the aforementioned conversation about the checked bag situation at the desk. Despite my very best efforts combining my Castilian Spanish and Geordie charm (we’re called Geordies where I’m from in the North East of England), the man at the check-in desk seemed to take real pleasure in explaining that the checked bag rules on my booking confirmation were irrelevant and I’d have to pay the fee.

For what it’s worth, Sky Priority check-in was also available at Mendoza.

Being nickel-and-dimed for a checked bag by a flag carrier airline is shameful.

Back at Aeroparque, there was no fast track, and the security line was ridiculously long. That said, it’s rare in South America to have fast track lanes. For example, no matter whether you’re flying economy or first class (even Air France La Première), everyone waits in the same line to clear pre-departure passport control at São Paulo’s Guarulhos.

Thanks to my Priority Pass, I did have access to the surprisingly nice AMAE lounge in the national departures part of the airport.

Even from the outside, my 15-year-old Embraer 190 looked like it had seen better days. The zebra-striped dirt streaks running from each window suggested this place hadn’t been washed or hit the maintenance hangar for a while.

Inside the Embraer, however, could have been a lot worse. The older seats had thick padding, and despite being a small 2-2-configured cabin, it felt bright and spacious.

It was the Uber advertising on every single headrest that I found most jarring.

The legroom was decent, too. The retro seatback screens, on the other hand, were pretty much redundant.

It was stepping on board the 16-year-old Boeing 737-700 back to Buenos Aires that Aerolíneas Argentinas’ low-costness was most glaring. Looking at this, I would never guess this plane belonged to a flag carrier. The seats were very uncomfortable, and I think I remember they didn’t recline either.

As for service, I don’t recall it being particularly good or particularly bad. Forgettable is probably the most accurate word.

Imagine the likes of Spirit (RIP) or Ryanair calling itself a national flag carrier; that’s basically what Aerolíneas Argentinas is. I’m planning a trip with my dad and brother for February next year that includes Argentina, and I will actively avoid flying Aerolíneas, even if it means forgoing the chance to earn any Flying Blue miles and XPs.

It’s almost as if the airline has been abandoned. After all, the only real competition is low-cost airlines at LATAM — the full-service carrier which dominates South America. Who knows, maybe things will change come 2028 when it takes delivery of new Airbus A330-900s and Boeing 737 MAXs.

If I were a power that be at SkyTeam, I’d definitely remove the airline from the alliance. And if I had my way, Aerolíneas Argentinas would be bought by LATAM, and the cherry on top would be LATAM joining SkyTeam. I should probably put a business case together for that…

I flew from GRU to LHR on BA in about 2018, first class redemption. I don't remember a long passport queue, but I do remember that I was escorted by the check-in agent from the desk to the lounge which I found surprising, but could explain the lack of issues. Have the rules changed, or have air France not worked out how to bypass the queue?

LATAM is no better. I had to fight tooth and nail with them at AEP over baggage allowances. I finally got a stupervisor and quoted actual tariff rules. She was a bit shocked and quickly backed off. Average Joe would not have not known what they were trying to pull. LATAM is just another ULCC that happens to fly international.

@Daniel--Welcome to OMAAT. I can understand your disappointment with AR. We value loyalty program status for what it takes to achieve it as well as its promised benefits. When those benefits are not delivered, one has a right to complain. However, I agree that your complaint likely should be with the FlyingBlue program, which issued your ticket. I haven't been to Argentina recently but years ago, I liked how convenient AEP was as compared to EZE, at least for domestic flights. Sorry to hear that the security lines are so long. My most recent foray into South America was to Chile, where I flew 4 domestic segments on LAN as a SkyTeam Elite+ member. All of the expected elite benefits were available to me and a companion on the same itineraries, i.e., I had none of the issues you described. So, your characterization of AR may be correct.

Hi Daniel! Great review but I’m afraid I might have to disagree a little with you here based on my personal experiences with AR this April and November. It is a shame that FB sent you an email that conflicted with AR’s policy. I suspect that it might be FB’s fault and not AR because it’s a standard email template. I flew with AR 4 times this year both domestically within Argentina and internationally. Their unconventional luggage allowance was stated quite clearly at online check-in. Unless you did not check in online or missed it ;). As for the checked luggage allowance in practice, I’ve found that it’s a YMMV situation. On 3 of my 4 legs with AR this year, the check-in agents accepted all the bags that I had paid for and the cabin bags that I had not. On my fourth leg AEP-IGR about two weeks ago (early Nov 2026), the agent told me that I had exceeded my allowance by one entire piece that weighed 8kg, which was unfortunate but fair. I had to pay the fee outside and it came up to US$10. Unlike you however, I did not have to go back in to show my EMD as proof of payment. It was automatically dispatched. I had some time at AEP and a chatty agent with whom I could practice my imperfect Argentine Spanish. She clarified with a few shrugs that there is no clear formula for calculating the fee. It seems to be a combination of fare class, date of booking mixed in with some Argentine chaos and charm. The maintenance issues, delays and their handling of irregular ops are two other stories altogether though.

#6194. Senators still see NDAA as chance for online safety legislation

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.

Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.

The Senate Judiciary Committee’s panel on Crime and Counterterrorism held the hearing after its Chairman Josh Hawley, R-Mo., and ranking member Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., introduced a bill Monday that would ban pre-dispute arbitration agreements from affecting cases where a minor was harmed online, including by sexual exploitation.

Hawley and Durbin also worked together on a separate bill to expand eligibility for victims of abuse to bring civil suits against online platforms that intentionally, knowingly or recklessly promoted or facilitated the abuse. It would also include penalties for certain platforms that fail to report child pornography violations on their sites.

That bill is included in a manager’s amendment to the Senate’s fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill. Durbin encouraged Congress to pass the NDAA “in the closing days” of the session because “protecting children is an important part of it.”

“I have a few weeks left in my service in the United States Senate,” said Durbin, who is retiring at the end of his term in January. “I’m thinking each day it’s coming to an end, but I want it to come [to an] end the right way.”

The subcommittee has spent much of the 119th Congress focused on harms to children online, including from artificial intelligence chatbots.

Tuesday’s hearing included testimony from survivors and experts on child exploitation on Roblox.

Hawley said that victims are bound by pre-dispute agreements with Roblox to settle claims through private arbitration, rather than in court.

“They slam the courthouse door shut in their faces,” Hawley said. “We’re talking about children now, child victims of sexual exploitation online are denied their day in court by the very company that has exposed them to the content to begin with.”

A spokesperson for Roblox said in a statement that “safety has been central” to the platform since its launch.

“We require age checks for chat, place users under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat,” the spokesperson said. “A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a company’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety.”

Myriam Gilles, a professor of law at Northwestern University, told the panel that a 2022 law that ended forced arbitration agreements for victims of sexual assault has gaps. She said Roblox has argued it does not apply to online actions, just “completed physical assault” and does not apply to platforms.

She also said that Hawley’s new arbitration bill would enhance the effects of his measure regarding civil suits by making sure those suits can be heard publicly if families so choose.

“Congress can pass laws, but if [suits] just get shunted into private arbitration, they’re doing no good in the world,” Gilles said. “A right to sue that ends in secret arbitration is a right in name only.”

The hearing came the same day that advocates, including reality TV personality and activist Paris Hilton, held a press conference to urge House action on a bill (S 1837) that would allow individuals to bring civil suits over nonconsensual intimate depictions generated by artificial intelligence or for possession or production of deepfake porn if there was also intent to disclose the images.

That bill passed the Senate in January but has not been taken up in the House.

Citi Shop takes some of the work out of saving money online. Once you've installed its browser extension, it acts as a shopping portal and coupon hunter all-in-one, rewarding you with statement credits.

It has broad reach, too, with more than 5,000 participating online merchants. That's easier than a traditional online shopping portal, which requires you to remember to start at the portal and click through before filling your cart.

Its ease of use makes it a great resource, but other portals or special discounts may save you more.

Here's how Citi Shop works and what to consider to determine if it's the best savings path for you.

Citi Shop is a free browser extension for primary cardholders with an eligible Citi credit card, including ThankYou points cards and cobranded cards. Citi retail and commercial cards are usually ineligible.

Offers come as either a percentage back or a fixed amount back, and your earnings are applied as a statement credit on the Citi card you selected during enrollment.

Citi Shop is separate from Citi Merchant Offers, which requires you to enroll in targeted offers with a specific Citi card and then use that card for the qualifying purchase.

Both Citi Shop and traditional portals give you an extra reward for making purchases they track.

But Citi Shop brings potential rebates to you, rather than requiring you to initiate your savings search. The extension automatically displays a pop-up with an available offer when you visit a participating website. You'll have the option to activate the offer before checkout.

All of Citi Shop's rebates are provided as statement credits, unlike the potential airline miles, hotel points or credit card rewards of traditional portals.

What I like about Citi Shop is that it also acts like a shopping assistant. Instead of opening six coupon sites only to discover that every code expired last Tuesday, it handles the scavenger hunt for you and tests available promo codes on your behalf.

Like Capital One Shopping, Citi Shop uses a browser extension. However, Capital One Shopping doesn't require a Capital One card to enroll and its rewards can be redeemed for eligible gift cards instead of a statement credit.

Generally speaking, Citi Shop clashes with other shopping portals. Both work by referring and tracking your purchase, so they can be mutually exclusive. You'll need to make your purchase through whichever offer is better.

Related: Chase shopping portal guide: How to earn bonus Ultimate Rewards points

Unless Citi Shop finds a promo code, it won't lower your total at checkout. Its returns arrive later as statement credits and may require patiently waiting two to six months, sometimes longer.

Even though you need an eligible Citi card to enroll, you don’t have to pay with it. Citi allows any payment method accepted by the merchant.

I really appreciate the flexibility to choose the best card for each purchase. For electronics, I might pick a card with an extended warranty while I might stick to a travel rewards credit card for hotel bookings. You can even pay with a gift card if you wish.

Regardless of how you pay, the statement credit will post to the Citi card you enrolled.

If you have an eligible Citi card but rarely remember to click through a shopping portal, Citi Shop is an easy win. Install it, activate offers when the pop-up appears and let the credits come to you. That convenience can also be a big benefit if you have partners or other family members who aren't as motivated to strategize on rewards as you are.

But with a little extra effort, you might be able to earn even more. When the Citi Shop pop-up appears with an offer, take a minute to compare before you click Activate.

Checking a shopping portal aggregator such as Cashback Monitor shows payouts from multiple cash-back, airline and credit card portals, making it easier to compare a Citi Shop statement credit with points or miles elsewhere.

Suppose a $200 jacket is marked down to $160. Citi Shop finds a $10 coupon, bringing the checkout price to $150, and offers 8% back. Assuming the full amount qualifies, you'd receive a $12 Citi Shop credit. If you pay with a card that earns 2% back and has an activated merchant offer for $5 off a $100 purchase, you'd collect another $8. After all the credits and rewards post, your net cost would be $130.

Read the terms before getting too excited. Some brands, products, gift cards or coupon codes may be excluded and you might not be able to stack every layer every time. Still, you can often use multiple discounts simultaneously for a better deal.

Citi Shop is not a program for instant gratification. Citi says statement credits post 61 to 180 days after a completed purchase, though some can take longer.

In many cases, offers may show as pending long before they officially pay out, to account for potential returns. Hotel rewards may remain pending until after the stay. Eventually, you'll see it on your statement as "CITI SHOP STATEMENT CREDIT."

If a credit hasn't posted after the expected window, contact Citi using the number on the back of your enrolled card. You may want to keep good records along the way, like a screenshot of the offer and an e-receipt from the purchase.

Citi Shop's biggest advantage is convenience. It does the heavy lifting by reminding you to activate offers so you don't miss out on earnings from your online orders, while testing coupon codes along the way. The offers themselves may or may not be the highest available, but they are certainly the easiest.

To truly optimize your returns, you'll want to compare Citi Shop earnings with those from other shopping portals — and stack other forms of saving along the way. But when that sounds like too much, the ease of this extension can still be a great way to tack on some extra returns.

#6192. Rove Launches Shopping Offers Of Up To 25 Miles Per Dollar—Why Brands Will Pay So Much To Win Your Business

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

Rove is launching personalized shopping offers of up to 25 miles per dollar on November 20. Connect your card accounts, activate an offer, and the program can give you a higher earning rate based on your shopping history.

If you buy from Nike, Adidas may be willing to spend real money to win your next purchase. That’s the example I reported from Rove’s presentation at the oneworld Loyalty Summit in September. CEO Max Morganroth described targeted merchant commissions reaching 40%. This puts that pitch in front of consumers, with an established advertising company helping supply the offers.

Rove says members will find personalized offers in the ‘For You’ section of its website and app after connecting their card accounts. Enhanced offers will display the standard earning rate alongside the higher rate.

They’re also expanding in-store earning to hundreds of participating physical retailers. Activate an eligible offer before buying, pay with the connected card, and the purchase gets tracked when the charge clears. Rove says miles will typically post within seven days.

These are selected offers reaching up to 25x, and Rove tells me merchants can change from month to month, and the same merchant might offer one person 5x and another 20x depending on whom it wants to reach.

Rove began rolling out in-store shopping alongside its app, dining program and instant gift card rewards in August. The new pieces are the personalized enhanced rates and broader retail coverage.

A shopping portal generally earns a commission for sending a merchant a sale. Better targeting can make that referral worth more.

Someone who regularly spends money in a category, but buys from a competitor, is a prospect worth reaching. So is someone who used to shop at a store and stopped. A merchant might pay to bring that person back, get an occasional customer to make another visit, or encourage a larger purchase.

The best prospect isn’t necessarily the biggest spender. It’s the person whose spending the offer can profitably change. Adidas gains little from paying a committed Adidas customer a huge rebate on shoes they were already going to buy. And it doesn’t much from showing a Nike loyalist an offer they’ll never use.

Rewards provider Valuedynamx describes a retailer campaign that gave new shoppers stronger incentives, lapsed shoppers offers to bring them back, and loyal customers smaller rewards. Its case study reports a 20.2% incremental sales lift among lapsed customers and 13.3% among new ones.

Targeting also lets a brand offer a substantial rebate without cutting the public price for everyone. It can spend more to win a customer it wants while avoiding an expensive storewide sale.

Cardlytics announced its Rove partnership on October 6, giving Rove access to its offers program. Rove brings an audience motivated by travel rewards. Cardlytics brings merchant campaigns and purchase-based targeting.

Rove’s program terms name Cardlytics and Plaid. Members can connect eligible debit or credit accounts through Plaid, and Cardlytics uses account transactions for targeting, reporting and measurement. Rove tells me its partners process the last 24 months of transaction history so merchants can target offers. Rove itself says it neither stores nor interacts with that history.

That history can reveal which merchants you use, how recently you’ve shopped, how often you return and how much you spend.

The policy also says Rove’s browser extension matches participating stores locally and doesn’t transmit your browsing history.

For the Cardlytics offers, personal identifiers are removed, but permit aggregated marketing insights, transaction-level validation and licensing transaction data to partners. There Are Already Several Versions Of This Chase Media Solutions uses purchase history to select offers for new, lapsed and existing customers through Chase Offers. Amex Offers is another familiar way to receive targeted rewards for qualifying purchases on an enrolled card. Capital One Shopping can use browsing, product and purchase information to personalize offers. Its rewards redeem for gift cards. The separate Capital One Offers available through Capital One accounts includes online and in-store offers, with payouts that can be miles, cash back or statement credits. Bilt’s neighborhood rewards and airline dining programs are other familiar ways to earn from merchant relationships using cards you already have. SimplyMiles is also activated offers that then earn American Airlines miles and Loyalty Points. Rove‘s appeal is the combination of earning rates, transferable miles and travel redemption options. I’ve written about redeeming its miles for Loyalty Eligible hotel stays while still earning hotel points and elite credit. #6191. End Of An Era: American Retires Boeing 777 Flagship First Class

American Airlines has just officially “retired” its Flagship First product on the Boeing 777-300ER, meaning that no US carrier offers an international first class product anymore. The good news is that an updated business class product is in the process of being rolled out, and that’s something that should benefit a lot of travelers.

As I’ve covered in the past, American is in the process of eliminating its “premium” first class product, and that change was just implemented for flights as of this week on the carrier’s biggest planes.

Specifically, the Boeing 777-300ER is American’s “flagship” aircraft, with 20 of the planes in the fleet. As of this week, the airline is no longer selling first class on these planes. Now, plenty of 777-300ERs with these cabins are still flying around, as American has just started reconfiguring its 777-300ERs with new cabins, including the new business class.

Still, for flights effective immediately, first class seats are just being sold as standard business class seats, and any business class passenger can select seats in the first two rows (you’d think they’d try to charge extra or at least reserve them for select elite members, but nope). So there will no longer be a differentiated soft product… not that there was much of a difference as of late anyway!

I expect we’ll continue to see these planes flying around well into late 2027, or possibly even into 2028, depending on how fast the retrofit project happens. American’s dedicated first class ground product has also largely been discontinued, as Flagship First Dining has turned into Flagship Dining, so a la carte lounge dining is now available to eligible business class passengers as well.

It’s great that these planes will be getting new business class suites, as they’ll also be the aircraft belonging to a US carrier with the most business class seats, as they’ll have 70 of them… that’s lot!

While American has now eliminated its international first class product, it’s worth emphasizing that the airline still technically has a “premium” first class, in the sense of a cabin above business class.

Specifically, American still has its specially configured Airbus A321T aircraft, which are used primarily for flights between New York (JFK) and Los Angeles (LAX) and San Francisco (SFO). The planes have 10 reverse herringbone seats spread across five rows, in a 1-1 configuration.

American also plans to eliminate this product, as the A321Ts will be reconfigured into standard A321 domestic configuration aircraft, and A321XLRs will be taking over the transcon routes.

American has stopped selling first class on these planes for flights as of March 28, 2027. After that date we’ll still see some of the planes flying with the cabins, but the first class seats will simply be sold as business class.

American Airlines has officially eliminated its international first class product, as Boeing 777-300ERs no longer have Flagship First for sale. These planes are being retrofitted, as first class seats are being eliminated, and new business class suites are being introduced. However, the planes will keep flying around with the current cabins for quite some time, and business class passengers can freely assign the first class seats.

In the spring, we’ll see American eliminate its last “premium” first class product, which is the A321T first class cabin, as those planes are replaced by A321XLRs.

What do you make of the end of American’s Flagship First on the 777?

#6189. Why International First Class Has Failed At US Airlines (But Shouldn’t)

We’ve just seen American formally retire its Boeing 777 first class, and with that, no airline in the United States has a “true” international first class anymore. It’s the end of an era, because going back many decades, premium products were largely pioneered by US carriers. So I think this raises the question — why can US carriers not make first class work in a way that’s economically viable, especially as they keep talking about how premium they are?

Before we get into this, let me make sure we’re all on the same page when it comes to terms. This post isn’t about the premium cabin on domestic flights, which is often referred to as first class. Instead, it’s about international flights that have a cabin above business class, when it’s marketed as first class. So this would include airlines on my list of the world’s best first class products.

Airline executives are divided on the merits of having an international first class cabin. Some insist that there’s no need for such a cabin, as business class has improved so much. Meanwhile others absolutely see merit to such a product.

I mean, just look at how carriers like Air France, Lufthansa, Singapore Airlines, and SWISS, are all investing in first class. I think Air France’s La Premiere first class is the perfect example of the upside such a product has for an airline:

What’s interesting is that for the airlines that succeed with first class, the single biggest market — and single biggest point of sale — is the United States. So how is it that carriers like Air France, Lufthansa, SWISS, etc., can make money offering first class to the United States (primarily targeting Americans), but US airlines seemingly can’t?

The US has way too many people with tens or hundreds of millions of dollars, or even billions of dollars. There are plenty of people who would pay to fly private, and would pay for Air France La Premiere first class, but would never consider paying the high price for first class on a US carrier, because it’s just not worth it.

When they fly first class, they want this…

It’s no surprise that first class at US carriers has historically failed. In many ways, it reflects the failures of the industry from decades past. In other words, first class has long been thought of as “upgrade class,” rather than something actually worth paying for. US carriers have managed to change that narrative on domestic flights, but not so much on international flights.

What explains the failure of first class at US carriers? If you ask me, here are the main factors:

Call it a hot take, but I think international first class absolutely could succeed at a US carrier, if done right, with a couple of caveats. Let me start with the two main hurdles that would need to be overcome, and I’ll acknowledge, this might just be the biggest issue:

If those hurdles could be overcome, here’s the play, as I see it (and yes, this is largely inspired by Air France La Premiere):

I think the halo effect of something like this would be massive as well. Seriously, US airline executives love to talk about how premium they are, but they can’t even introduce a top-end product, despite having access to the most lucrative customer base in the world.

In terms of economics, let me also point out that the opportunity cost of a first class cabin isn’t actually that high. “Premium” is all the rage, so what you do here is eliminate some economy seats:

At this point, no airline from the United States offers first class on international flights anymore. For airlines that can’t stop talking about how unbelievably premium they are, I find that to be a pretty perplexing reality. I know that many people have just accepted “oh, a good business class is the future,” but I have a different take.

I think no US carrier actually being able to offer a globally competitive product is a failure in strategy and creativity. They have access to the world’s most lucrative customer base, and other airlines can seemingly make money serving US customers with a first class product. The issue is, US carriers have long not actually given people a reason to fly first class, all while offering too much capacity.

Personally I think there would be a lot of merit to an international first class product that’s boutique, and is operated in the right markets. That’s not to say that I think it’ll happen — I don’t — but I do think it could succeed. The only real hurdle to overcome would be how to ensure good service…

What’s your take on the possible merit of US carriers offering first class?

The main issue with international first class on US carriers is that it's international (for once the American obsession with the word is relevant :)), therefore competition from non-US carrier exists. US simply doesn't have service culture on level needed to deliver true premium experience, and it's twice as true in aviation. Internally it works because you have various lackluster products competing against each other, but no one sane will pay top buck for an AA experience when they can fly AF. This consequently leaves US airlines with the more price sensitive segment, which simply doesn't work in first class.

One thing to look at is that any top product sits at the top of the iceberg. And it has thus to be credible with respect of the rest of the iceberg. You can't sell a Coco Chanel Suite in a shabby 3 class Hotel, even if the suite itself has all the bells and whistles. The US airlines would not have to just deliver a good first class they would have to improve their other premium products too.

From a French perspective, the failure of US international First Class goes way beyond airline economics, it’s a cultural impossibility. Money buys convenience and private jets, not elegance. You see it every day in how Americans travel abroad: loud, sacrificing elegance on the altar of comfort, boarding premium cabins in Juicy Couture tracksuits. True First Class requires discretion, quiet refinement, and centuries of art de vivre and hospitality heritage. Without that DNA, a US carrier can never deliver a genuine First Class experience, just an oversized Business Class. 😉

US airlines (which do not have a long range approach) have spent 10 years building business class only not to start degrading it with “basic” business fares. Psycho strategy in action.

I'm not one who can justify to myself the cost of a revenue long-haul FC ticket, but I can see why some people might. Like US airlines, Qantas offers fewer first-class cabins than in the past, and they are absent from newer jets. They currently offer 14 F seats on A380 flights to LAX, DFW, LHR, JNB and SIN from Sydney. First is coming back on the new A350-1000ULR aircraft slated for their flagship Sydney to New York and London non-stop routes, with six seats. Those aircraft will also operate some other routes. I doubt Qantas decided this lightly. I've flown first on QF12 from LAX (on points, quite a lot of them), and the difference from J was noticeable, I can see why people would pay for it, and I would repeat (for points). On my flight, the cabin was full. Looking at the next few months, award F seats to and from the US are not unicorns, but they are not common. There are none available on QF1 to LHR or SIN. I suspect there's going to be a halo effect from these extreme long-haul flights, and a second from them offering first class. What that will be worth remains to be seen. Whether QF or the US3 have made the better business decision also remains to be seen.

#6188. Southwest Airlines Passenger Was Kicked Off When Her Husband Didn’t Board The Plane—Even Though She Offered To Pay

A Southwest Airlines passenger says she was settled into an exit row window seat in Las Vegas, pleased about the empty middle seat beside her, when the crew began looking for her husband. He wasn’t coming—and she was traveling on his Companion Pass. Angie Batis says she offered to buy her own ticket, using a credit card or points, but was told it was too late. Instead, she was escorted off the roughly 9 p.m. flight to Boise and quoted about $400 for a departure the next morning. Southwest was right about the Companion Pass rule. Surely though it shouldn’t take materially longer to sell a ticket than to remove a passenger. She’d spent four days in Las Vegas, checked two 50 pound bags, and was ready to get home. Sitting in row 14, she’d already given the flight attendant her verbal agreement to help with the emergency exit. Her headphones were on. She was listening to an audiobook and playing a game on her phone. Then came the announcement asking Mr. Batis to identify himself. She told the crew he wasn’t on board and wouldn’t be joining them. That’s when she realized why the middle seat was empty. An employee came back to her row and explained that her free ticket depended on her husband actually taking the flight. Well, can I just pay with a credit card? … I’ve been a Southwest card member for 20 plus years. I have my own points. Can I just book it, you know, pay for it now? She says he told her they were ready to push back. He left, returned about three minutes later, and told her she’d have to get off. She gathered her things and went with him. I think he was expecting, like, some complete chaos. @angiebatis — Her account of being removed from the Southwest flight Companion Pass Requires The Passholder To Travel I’ve been a Companion Pass holder, including through promotions, and it’s still an extraordinary deal. Book your own Southwest flight with money or points, then add your designated companion for taxes and fees starting at $5.60 each way, as long as there’s a seat available. The free travel is tied to accompanying the passholder. Her husband paid for a ticket, which then supports the companion’s ticket. The rules though are very clear: If the Companion is not traveling with the Member, the Companion’s reservation will be canceled. I’ve covered almost this exact situation before. In June 2024, a companion boarded Southwest flight 2097 from Savannah to Baltimore. The passholder canceled his own ticket just before departure. Southwest removed the companion, conducting a manual boarding pass check to find her in the days before assigned seating. That case involved a cancellation and an apparent attempt to get the companion transported while refunding the underlying ticket. Here the passenger was fully willing to pay. I don’t think she was actually trying to scam the airline, though she’d be traveling free (and if her husband did cancel in time prior to departure he’d still have his flight credit to use). The requirement to fly together isn’t one of the changes Southwest is making to Companion Pass in 2027. It’s been a longstanding requirement. She Offered To Pay For The Seat Comments on the woman’s video between people who think a longtime Southwest customer should know how the pass works and people who think the airline should have found a way to get her home. It’s probably just best that she got off without making a scene. Several viewers ask why this wasn’t caught at check-in or at the gate. But checking in isn’t the same as boarding. If her husband wasn’t checked in though it should get caught at the check-in deadline. He may have been checked in and just didn’t board. There’s an interesting bit of history here. This same woman went viral in 2024 praising a Southwest gate agent in Phoenix. She filmed herself thanking an employee named Krista for her kindness. In this video, she also thanks the gate agent and tells her it isn’t her fault. Her host at the Venetian arranged a chauffeur, another room, dinner and a car back to the airport. She was still separated from her checked bags, without a phone charging cord or a brush. I bet her casino host could manage that… So this was day old hair yesterday. Today it’s two day old hair. …I was embarrassed, I was humiliated, I was mad at my husband, the whole thing. (HT: Paddle Your Own Kanoo) Topics on this pageAirline PassengerSouthwest AirlinesBaltimoreBoiseLas VegasPhoenixThe Venetian+5 more More From View from the Wing

She should have had a full fare and cancelation of the companion pass as repercussions.

Can’t travel as a free companion without the person who earned the companion pass. They know this. The time to rectify the situation is not when the plane is boarded. It’s before you board. Just like when people want to upgrade seats after they board. They could have done it when they booked. They could have done it in the app. They could have done it at the ticket counter. They could have done it in the gate area. But suddenly it is an emergency once they have boarded because they didn’t plan ahead?

“A Southwest Airlines passenger says she was settled into an exit row window seat in Las Vegas, pleased about the empty middle seat beside her…”

“Then came the announcement asking Mr. Batis to identify himself. She told the crew he wasn’t on board and wouldn’t be joining them. That’s when she realized why the middle seat was empty.”

She knew her husband wasn’t traveling and THAT’S when she realized why the seat next to her was empty?

Finally rules are being enforced, she knew she was in the wrong. Should have just got off the plane and went to nearest ticket counter to buy a ticket and not expected airline to accommodate her an “already” on the plane ticket.

#6187. Hill GOP looking to trim White House's $50 billion aviation ask

Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s new ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.

The original ask contained roughly $12 billion that was tied directly to air traffic control upgrades, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said, with the remainder going toward long-sought airport terminal and other upgrades to aging aviation facilities.

Duffy and Vought laid out in a letter to House and Senate appropriators on Tuesday what the extra $20 billion would be for — half for construction of five new air route traffic control centers, and half for construction, replacement and improvement of up to 140 air traffic control towers.

They justified the increased demand because of the “urgent need” that became evident after the ground stop. Duffy and Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford fanned out across the Capitol to try to sell the request, including a stop at Senate Republicans’ weekly policy lunch.

But it quickly became evident that their own allies on Capitol Hill want more and better justification for why so much extra money is needed.

Not only are there concerns that much of the request would go to terminal reconstruction and other longer-term projects, but lawmakers keep noting the FAA hasn’t yet spent about $8 billion out of the initial $12.5 billion “down payment” on air traffic control modernization provided in last year’s budget reconciliation law.

“I don’t think the full $50 billion will be funded,” Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said Tuesday. “What we just discussed there, and what I expressed, is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization.”

Still, Cruz said the administration had done a “good job” with the initial $12.5 billion modernization plan so far and he expected to see continued bipartisan support for the effort.

Senate Republicans are considering adding additional aviation funds through a filibuster-proof reconciliation bill, a process that could begin as soon as this week with a floor “vote-a-rama” on a resolution to unlock that process. Cruz said that while reconciliation could be the vehicle used, additional aviation funds need to be “safety-focused.”

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said after the lunch with Duffy and Bedford that he expects Congress will look at a package more in the $10 billion to $30 billion range.

For his part, Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., said the airline industry itself should foot at least a portion of the bill, considering how much federal support the carriers have received over the years.

“I don't understand why the airline industry doesn't pay for it. We give them unbelievable amounts of money,” Scott said, adding that he doesn’t like adding to the deficit and is “not big on government running things.”

Duffy explained the need for the high price tag as the result of decades of pent-up demand that are now threatening major disruptions and safety risks to the traveling public.

“This has never been done. To be clear, we are keeping planes safe in the sky, and we are switching out equipment that’s been a problem for decades,” he said. “I and the president have decided we are going to lean in and fix it.”

He called the effort a “historic investment” reflecting the ways air travel has changed since much of the nation’s infrastructure was built — noting that the newest tower was constructed in 1969 and much of the software being used is from the 1990s. Still, Duffy said, on the current course of funding, it would take 300 years to replace every U.S. tower.

“I'm not going to tell [Congress] how to do their work, but I'm telling everybody what we need,” Duffy said. “And whether it's a party-line vote or if it's a bipartisan vote, I do think this is one moment in a very charged political environment — one moment where almost all Americans and bipartisan members of both bodies are kind of in agreement that we should lean in to do this.”

Even as Duffy petitioned for additional funds Tuesday, he said that the “root cause” of the equipment instability that made the ground stop necessary is still unclear as investigators analyze the router that caused the problem.

A “routine switchover” from old copper wires to digital fiber in the telecommunications system “started to create issues in our network,” Duffy explained Tuesday.

The telecommunications transition includes the conversion of thousands of routers to what are known as Juniper devices — a process being undertaken by contractor L3Harris Technologies. Duffy and Bedford explained that 68 other routers had been converted without incident prior to the problematic switchover Friday.

Bedford said Tuesday that use of the router that officials have identified as the source of the system instability has been suspended “and we've disabled the ones that are out there.”

The decision to suspend use of the router followed an inquiry sent to the agency by Senate Commerce Committee Democrats a day prior. “With thousands of conversions remaining, FAA must address outstanding safety and reliability concerns before expanding installation,” they wrote.

Bedford said he was “highly confident” that similar problems wouldn’t erupt again. “Every element of this is going to be analyzed to see what we learn here and make sure that it doesn't get repeated,” he said.

David Jordan, Lia Chien and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

Washingtonians have a new option to Portugal next summer.

TAP Air Portugal will launch a new thrice-weekly service from Dulles International Airport (IAD) to Porto Airport (OPO) on March 30, 2027. Westbound flights will operate on Wednesdays, Fridays and Saturdays through the summer, and on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays beginning in October.

TAP, a Star Alliance partner of United Airlines, will fly an Airbus A321LR on the new IAD-OPO route. The long-range, single-aisle aircraft is fitted with 16 lie-flat business-class seats and 155 economy seats.

The new Portugal route is the latest international addition at IAD. United plans to launch new service to Toulouse, France, in April and to Milan in May, using its new long-range A321XLR on the former route.

International seats from IAD will increase nearly 7% in the first six months of 2027 compared to this year, schedule data from aviation analytics firm Cirium shows.

IAD is undergoing a massive, $22 billion redevelopment to bring its infrastructure up to modern standards. The first piece — a 14-gate section of the new Concourse E that includes a new, large United Club — opened earlier in November. Future phases include a new international arrivals facility that would support additional long-haul growth.

And if the redevelopment plan stays on schedule, IAD could retire its jet-age mobile lounges by the mid-2030s.

TAP’s new OPO route complements its existing service to IAD from Lisbon Airport (LIS).

The state-owned Portuguese airline is in the process of being privatized as part of the Lufthansa Group. The German airline conglomerate plans to buy an initial 44.9% stake in TAP, aiming to close the deal by the first quarter of 2028.

Lufthansa Group chief commercial officer Dieter Vranckx said in October that once the TAP deal is done, Lufthansa intends to integrate the Portuguese airline into its transatlantic joint venture with Air Canada and United.

#6185. Why I’d Pick Economy Over Premium Economy On An Overnight Flight

I just got back to Rio after a quick trip to Ireland for Aer Lingus’ event to showcase their new A330 cabins, including its first-ever premium economy.

I flew Air France economy both ways, and I’m glad I resisted the offer of $420 during online check-in to upgrade the outbound overnight economy leg. Ironically, it was the long day-flight back where I actually wished I’d upgraded.

However, to answer the economy vs. premium economy question, it all comes down to maximising comfort, and I think this is easier to do in economy than premium economy.

If, like me, sleeping upright or on your back is almost impossible, then what follows will likely apply to you.

The main reason I’m deterred to pick premium economy for overnight flights is because of the fixed armrests, where tray tables are sometimes stowed in this cabin.

Despite the extra recline and leg rest element (which sometimes makes it even harder to get comfortable), the fixed armrests restrict the ability to sleep any way other than straight like a pencil.

To make matters worse, they stop you from lying across more than one seat if you find yourself in an empty row.

It’s for that reason that I much prefer economy. While having a row to yourself isn’t guaranteed, there’s at least a chance of being able to move around the cabin, or stretch out into an empty seat. No matter where you sit or how empty the cabin is, you can’t do that in premium economy.

Another element of my pre-trip planning that I expect many of you to relate to is the fact it takes me so long umming and aahing over the best seat to pick.

Thanks to my Flying Blue Gold status (SkyTeam Elite Plus), I could pick any seat in the economy cabin of the Boeing 777-200ER for free from 72 hours before departure.

I narrowed it down to an empty seat in the exit row, and the only row of three with an empty middle seat. I didn’t even consider one of the many empty middle rows of four seats in case they filled up before take off and I ended up in an aisle with no window to rest my head. Using the window or plane’s fuselage to rest my head on is the only saving grace for me when trying to sleep sitting upright.

As the empty exit seat would have the same restricting fixed partition as premium, I decided against that, too.

After the “boarding complete” announcement was made, the middle seat in my row remained empty, and there were three seats free in the middle of row 25, a row in front. I explained to the girl in the aisle seat that if one of us moved to the other row, we’d both have three seats to ourselves. She didn’t seem to understand my point, and said she’d prefer to sit in the aisle than us both have three free seats to ourselves.

I didn’t want to move to the middle seats either, so I got as comfortable as I could using the middle seat and the pillow I brought from home.

In the end, I did manage to get some half decent curled up shut eye (the thick pillow protected my back from the hard parts of the seat when propped against the fuselage). However, when I went to the loo, I noticed some people in the rear cabin had got lucky and were fast asleep spread across a whole four seats.

Maybe I’ll take more of a risk next time…

I’m not saying economy is always a better choice than premium. For example, I’d always recommend Emirates’ pretty darn impressive premium economy over economy, because it genuinely is several steps up from economy.

If it was up to me, I’d have had a lie-flat seat for the overnight segment. I didn’t, and I’m pretty certain I got better sleep quality curled up across two seats in economy that I would have almost upright on my back in premium.

Would you ever choose economy over premium economy?
