#6184. Bilt Offers JetBlue Elite Status For December Rent Day—With A Fast Track To Keep It Through 2027

Bilt’s December Rent Day offers a three month trial of JetBlue elite status, with a much easier path to keeping it through January 2028. Silver and Gold members get Mosaic 1 at no points cost. Platinum members start at Mosaic 2, which means EvenMore seats at booking instead of waiting until closer to departure. When Bilt added JetBlue as a transfer partner last month, I wrote that status matches could be coming. You qualify based on your Bilt status, so you don’t need to bring elite status from another airline. There’s also up to a 100% bonus redeeming Bilt points for credit card statement credits, a targeted spending offer, and Brittany Snow playing Rent Free. I have no idea who she is. I’m much more interested in the JetBlue offer than cashing out Bilt points at under 1.5 cents apiece. Three Months Of JetBlue Status, With A Path Through January 2028 Here’s the initial status offered: Bilt Status   JetBlue Trial Status   Points Requirement Blue Mosaic 1 10,000 Bilt points Silver Mosaic 1 None Gold Mosaic 1 None Platinum Mosaic 2 None Blue members have to transfer 10,000 points to trigger the match. Everyone has three months after receiving the matched status to earn and receive enough qualifying tiles to extend it through January 31, 2028: Status Earned   Challenge Requirement   Normal Annual Requirement Mosaic 1 10 tiles 50 tiles Mosaic 2 25 tiles 100 tiles Mosaic 3 40 tiles 150 tiles Under JetBlue’s normal earning rules, a tile takes $100 in qualifying spending on flights, JetBlue Vacations or TrueBlue Travel, or $1,000 in JetBlue credit card spending. So the travel equivalents are $1,000, $2,500 and $4,000. Taxes and fees don’t count. The corresponding spend amounts would be $10,000, $25,000 and $40,000, or you could combine tiles from travel and card spending. Spending on a Bilt card isn’t JetBlue card spending. You can earn JetBlue tiles via travel on JetBlue, United Airlines, JetBlue Vacations; cobrand card spend; purchased or earned bonus tiles (but gifted tiles don’t count); and the annual 25 Tile Bonus awarded to JetBlue Premier Wcardmembers. Folks who have received a past JetBlue challenge are eligible for this offer. Where The Status Is Most Useful The immediate value is better seating and fewer fees on trips you already intend to take. Mosaic 1 includes one checked bag, priority services, eligible same-day switches, and complimentary EvenMore selection starting 36 hours before departure for the member and up to two companions, subject to availability. Mosaic 2 adds a second checked bag and moves EvenMore selection to booking for the member and up to two companions. Mosaic 3 includes four Premium Upgrade Certificates, the new name for Move to Mint certificates (and those meeting the challenge requirements will receive them). Main Base fares exclude important seating benefits. And Mosaic 1 through 3 don’t include Mosaic 4 lounge access. JetBlue has also announced complimentary upgrades to its new BlueFirst domestic first class for all Mosaic tiers as equipped aircraft enter service. These are space available upgrades, with higher Mosaic levels ahead of lower ones. Main Base and EvenMore Base fares don’t qualify. Premium Upgrade Certificates can confirm Mint or BlueFirst, including on eligible TrueBlue points tickets. Four certificates don’t necessarily mean four upgrades because the number required varies by flight. Starting February 1, JetBlue will also let Mosaic 2 members select a certificate through Perks You Pick. I’ve asked whether matched members get that selection. There’s A United Airlines Angle, Too Under JetBlue’s Blue Sky partnership, Mosaic members receive benefits on eligible United Airlines trips booked through JetBlue, including a checked bag, preferred seats after booking and Economy Plus at check-in. Mosaic 1 gets Group 2 boarding, while Mosaic 2 and above get Group 1. United flights booked through JetBlue also earn tiles under the ordinary program. So you can keep JetBlue status through travel on United. There’s No Transfer Bonus Bilt points transfer to JetBlue at 1:1. This December announcement doesn’t include a bonus on those transfers. I’m generally not moving Bilt points to JetBlue for ordinary redemptions worth around 1.3 cents apiece. One option worth comparing is a regular paid JetBlue ticket purchased through Bilt’s portal using points. Under ordinary revenue-ticket rules, that should earn tiles, whereas transferring points into TrueBlue doesn’t earn tiles. Portal bookings do give up JetBlue’s direct-booking points bonus. The more interesting transfer uses remain partner business class awards, such as the 54,000-point Condor business class awards from the East Coast to Frankfurt I’ve covered, when available. Mosaic doesn’t add benefits to a Condor flight. If you already have the JetBlue Premier card, its 15% award rebate includes partner flights. A 54,000-point award returns 8,100 TrueBlue points, for a net cost of 45,900. You need all 54,000 upfront, and the rebate comes back as JetBlue points, not Bilt points. A 100% Statement Credit Bonus Still Only Gets You About 1.1 Cents Eligible cardholders get increased statement credit redemption value from November 20 at 9 a.m. Eastern through December 2 at 2:59 a.m. Eastern. The minimum redemption is 1,000 points. This bonus depends on which Bilt credit card you have, not your Bilt elite status. At the usual 0.55-cent statement credit redemption rate, the math is: Bilt Card   Bonus   Value Per Point   Credit For 10,000 Points Blue 25% 0.6875 cents $68.75 Obsidian 50% 0.825 cents $82.50 Palladium 100% 1.1 cents $110 I wouldn’t do this. Even Palladium’s doubled rate is less than the $125 in travel those same 10,000 points buy through Bilt, before considering Hyatt or airline transfers. I passed on last month’s gift card bonus, too. Two Separate Opportunities To Earn 1,000 Extra Points Some cardholders will receive a targeted offer for 1,000 bonus points after $500 in everyday purchases from November 20 at 9 a.m. Eastern through November 30 at 11:59 p.m. Eastern. Rent and mortgage payments don’t count. Check your account for eligibility. Then the usual Rent Day double points apply on December 1, with a cap of 1,000 additional points: Bilt Blue: 2 points per dollar on everyday spending. Bilt Obsidian: 6 points in your selected dining or grocery category, 4 on travel and 2 on other everyday spending. Bilt Palladium: 4 points per dollar on everyday spending. Rent and tax payments don’t qualify for the extra points (tax payments usually don’t earn at all). On Palladium, $500 in eligible December 1 spending earns the full 1,000-point Rent Day bonus on top of the usual 1,000 points. The holiday shopping offer ends the night before Rent Day. The same purchase can’t satisfy both offers. A targeted Palladium member with $500 of ordinary spending before the deadline and another $500 on December 1 could earn 2,000 promotional bonus points across the two. Brittany Snow, Free Rent And December Experiences Brittany Snow is this month’s Rent Free guest. The game opens November 20 at noon Eastern and closes December 1 at 3 p.m. Eastern, with results after 4 p.m. The top 10 members win a month’s rent up to $2,500, with additional rent winners depending on how well she does. Rent winners also get a signed copy of September Letters. The next 100 receive 1,000 points and the next 500 receive 100 points. There’s also a November 22 brunch with Snow and September Letters co-founder Jaspre Guest at The Twenty Two in New York, from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. It’s $45 or 3,000 points, includes bites and cocktails, and opens for booking November 20 at 9 a.m. Eastern. Guests must be at least 21. The booking is final sale. The book itself is $20 or 2,000 points, with 100 copies available beginning November 20 at 9 a.m. Eastern. Members can apply up to $20 of their monthly Bilt Cash allowance. I’d use available Bilt Cash rather than redeem points at a penny each. Shipping is expected in two to three weeks, and sales are final. Members can write letters through the app, choosing whether to keep them private or share them. Select Bilt Alliance buildings will also have September Letters mailboxes, with letters mailed back to their writers in a year. Bookings for the following experiences open Saturday, November 21 at 11:50 a.m. Eastern for Gold and Platinum, and noon for everyone else: Dining: December 1 meals at 40 restaurants across nine cities. Most cost $35–$78 or 2,500–5,000 points. There are three-course menus at most venues, four courses at Hutong and omakase at seven Bondi locations. Drink add-ons cost $20–$46 and must be purchased when booking. Up to $50 Bilt Cash can be applied to one dining experience, with the rest paid in cash. Book by November 30 at 5 p.m. Eastern. There’s also first access to American Cut’s December 31 cocktail party in New York at 6 p.m., priced at $250, with 20 seats. Comedy: 20 shows December 4–19. Club experiences cost $40 or 2,500 points, except Mic Drop MANIA in Chandler at $30 or 2,000 points, with two drinks included. Premium experiences cost $75 or 5,000 points and include two drinks and light bites. Austin’s The Creek & The Cave is among the venues. Members can use up to $50 Bilt Cash toward a comedy show for the month. Booking closes at 11 a.m. Eastern on the show date, or when sold out. Fitness: Free December 1 SoulCycle and Barry’s classes, with 1,175 and 580 spots respectively. Bookings close November 30 at 7 p.m. Eastern. Dining allows four seats per member per booking, and comedy allows four tickets per person. These experiences are final sale. I’d use Bilt Cash before points: a common $60 dinner costs 4,000 points, but applying $50 Bilt Cash leaves $10 to pay and keeps your points available for travel. And on December 1, Bilt’s cafe at 837 Washington Street in New York will offer members a complimentary Daniel Boulud tasting from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Eastern: lobster vol-au-vent (with a vegetarian option), warm apple chausson, a hot chocolate shake and warm spiced cider. JetBlue has also announced complimentary upgrades to its new BlueFirst domestic first class for all Mosaic tiers as equipped aircraft enter service. These are space available upgrades, with higher Mosaic levels ahead of lower ones. Main Base and EvenMore Base fares don’t qualify. Premium Upgrade Certificates can confirm Mint or BlueFirst, including on eligible TrueBlue points tickets. Four certificates don’t necessarily mean four upgrades because the number required varies by flight. Starting February 1, JetBlue will also let Mosaic 2 members select a certificate through Perks You Pick. I’ve asked whether matched members get that selection. There’s A United Airlines Angle, Too Under JetBlue’s Blue Sky partnership, Mosaic members receive benefits on eligible United Airlines trips booked through JetBlue, including a checked bag, preferred seats after booking and Economy Plus at check-in. Mosaic 1 gets Group 2 boarding, while Mosaic 2 and above get Group 1. United flights booked through JetBlue also earn tiles under the ordinary program. So you can keep JetBlue status through travel on United. There’s No Transfer Bonus Bilt points transfer to JetBlue at 1:1. This December announcement doesn’t include a bonus on those transfers. I’m generally not moving Bilt points to JetBlue for ordinary redemptions worth around 1.3 cents apiece. One option worth comparing is a regular paid JetBlue ticket purchased through Bilt’s portal using points. Under ordinary revenue-ticket rules, that should earn tiles, whereas transferring points into TrueBlue doesn’t earn tiles. Portal bookings do give up JetBlue’s direct-booking points bonus. The more interesting transfer uses remain partner business class awards, such as the 54,000-point Condor business class awards from the East Coast to Frankfurt I’ve covered, when available. Mosaic doesn’t add benefits to a Condor flight. If you already have the JetBlue Premier card, its 15% award rebate includes partner flights. A 54,000-point award returns 8,100 TrueBlue points, for a net cost of 45,900. You need all 54,000 upfront, and the rebate comes back as JetBlue points, not Bilt points. A 100% Statement Credit Bonus Still Only Gets You About 1.1 Cents Eligible cardholders get increased statement credit redemption value from November 20 at 9 a.m. Eastern through December 2 at 2:59 a.m. Eastern. The minimum redemption is 1,000 points. This bonus depends on which Bilt credit card you have, not your Bilt elite status. At the usual 0.55-cent statement credit redemption rate, the math is: Bilt Card   Bonus   Value Per Point   Credit For 10,000 Points Blue 25% 0.6875 cents $68.75 Obsidian 50% 0.825 cents $82.50 Palladium 100% 1.1 cents $110 I wouldn’t do this. Even Palladium’s doubled rate is less than the $125 in travel those same 10,000 points buy through Bilt, before considering Hyatt or airline transfers. I passed on last month’s gift card bonus, too. Two Separate Opportunities To Earn 1,000 Extra Points Some cardholders will receive a targeted offer for 1,000 bonus points after $500 in everyday purchases from November 20 at 9 a.m. Eastern through November 30 at 11:59 p.m. Eastern. Rent and mortgage payments don’t count. Check your account for eligibility. Then the usual Rent Day double points apply on December 1, with a cap of 1,000 additional points: Bilt Blue: 2 points per dollar on everyday spending. Bilt Obsidian: 6 points in your selected dining or grocery category, 4 on travel and 2 on other everyday spending. Bilt Palladium: 4 points per dollar on everyday spending. Rent and tax payments don’t qualify for the extra points (tax payments usually don’t earn at all). On Palladium, $500 in eligible December 1 spending earns the full 1,000-point Rent Day bonus on top of the usual 1,000 points. The holiday shopping offer ends the night before Rent Day. The same purchase can’t satisfy both offers. A targeted Palladium member with $500 of ordinary spending before the deadline and another $500 on December 1 could earn 2,000 promotional bonus points across the two. Brittany Snow, Free Rent And December Experiences Brittany Snow is this month’s Rent Free guest. The game opens November 20 at noon Eastern and closes December 1 at 3 p.m. Eastern, with results after 4 p.m. The top 10 members win a month’s rent up to $2,500, with additional rent winners depending on how well she does. Rent winners also get a signed copy of September Letters. The next 100 receive 1,000 points and the next 500 receive 100 points. There’s also a November 22 brunch with Snow and September Letters co-founder Jaspre Guest at The Twenty Two in New York, from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. It’s $45 or 3,000 points, includes bites and cocktails, and opens for booking November 20 at 9 a.m. Eastern. Guests must be at least 21. The booking is final sale. The book itself is $20 or 2,000 points, with 100 copies available beginning November 20 at 9 a.m. Eastern. Members can apply up to $20 of their monthly Bilt Cash allowance. I’d use available Bilt Cash rather than redeem points at a penny each. Shipping is expected in two to three weeks, and sales are final. Members can write letters through the app, choosing whether to keep them private or share them. Select Bilt Alliance buildings will also have September Letters mailboxes, with letters mailed back to their writers in a year. Bookings for the following experiences open Saturday, November 21 at 11:50 a.m. Eastern for Gold and Platinum, and noon for everyone else: Dining: December 1 meals at 40 restaurants across nine cities. Most cost $35–$78 or 2,500–5,000 points. There are three-course menus at most venues, four courses at Hutong and omakase at seven Bondi locations. Drink add-ons cost $20–$46 and must be purchased when booking. Up to $50 Bilt Cash can be applied to one dining experience, with the rest paid in cash. Book by November 30 at 5 p.m. Eastern. There’s also first access to American Cut’s December 31 cocktail party in New York at 6 p.m., priced at $250, with 20 seats. Comedy: 20 shows December 4–19. Club experiences cost $40 or 2,500 points, except Mic Drop MANIA in Chandler at $30 or 2,000 points, with two drinks included. Premium experiences cost $75 or 5,000 points and include two drinks and light bites. Austin’s The Creek & The Cave is among the venues. Members can use up to $50 Bilt Cash toward a comedy show for the month. Booking closes at 11 a.m. Eastern on the show date, or when sold out. Fitness: Free December 1 SoulCycle and Barry’s classes, with 1,175 and 580 spots respectively. Bookings close November 30 at 7 p.m. Eastern. Dining allows four seats per member per booking, and comedy allows four tickets per person. These experiences are final sale. I’d use Bilt Cash before points: a common $60 dinner costs 4,000 points, but applying $50 Bilt Cash leaves $10 to pay and keeps your points available for travel. And on December 1, Bilt’s cafe at 837 Washington Street in New York will offer members a complimentary Daniel Boulud tasting from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Eastern: lobster vol-au-vent (with a vegetarian option), warm apple chausson, a hot chocolate shake and warm spiced cider. Blue members have to transfer 10,000 points to trigger the match. Everyone has three months after receiving the matched status to earn and receive enough qualifying tiles to extend it through January 31, 2028:

Under JetBlue’s normal earning rules, a tile takes $100 in qualifying spending on flights, JetBlue Vacations or TrueBlue Travel, or $1,000 in JetBlue credit card spending. So the travel equivalents are $1,000, $2,500 and $4,000. Taxes and fees don’t count.

The corresponding spend amounts would be $10,000, $25,000 and $40,000, or you could combine tiles from travel and card spending. Spending on a Bilt card isn’t JetBlue card spending.

You can earn JetBlue tiles via travel on JetBlue, United Airlines, JetBlue Vacations; cobrand card spend; purchased or earned bonus tiles (but gifted tiles don’t count); and the annual 25 Tile Bonus awarded to JetBlue Premier Wcardmembers. Folks who have received a past JetBlue challenge are eligible for this offer.

#6183. Third Time’s Not The Charm: A SWISS A220’s Odd Triple Aborted Takeoff

If you’re a frequent flyer, odds are that you’ve encountered an aborted takeoff, whereby the plane accelerates down the runway, only to slow down, and eventually come to a stop. In some cases this can feel like a non-event, while in other cases it can feel much scarier, depending on the speed at which the takeoff is aborted.

However, here’s something you don’t often see — a SWISS Airbus A220 aborted its takeoff three times in a row, before finally returning to the gate to see what was going on, as reported by Blick. The explanation is actually quite logical, but that doesn’t make the whole ordeal any less unusual.

On Tuesday, November 17, 2026, SWISS flight LX2110 was scheduled to operate from Zurich (ZRH) to Malaga (AGP), with a 9:35AM departure. The flight was operated by an Airbus A220-300 with the registration code HB-JCM.

The plane pushed back and taxied out to the runway right on schedule. The pilots began the takeoff roll, but then quickly applied the brakes, causing the plane to come to a stop, while still at a slow speed. The pilots took a moment to run checklists, and then decided on another takeoff attempt, only for the same thing to happen again!

After the second aborted takeoff, the captain reportedly informed passengers that the thrust levers had popped out during the takeoff roll, and that was the reason for the aborted takeoff. However, rather than returning to the gate, they decided to attempt an additional takeoff roll.

Once again, the takeoff was aborted. At that point the captain explained that nothing like this had ever happened to him before in his 12 year career, and that the plane would be returning to the gate.

There ended up being a plane change, and then the A220 with the registration code HB-JCO was assigned to operate this flight — it ended up taking off at 1:29PM and landing at 3:52PM, around 3.5 hours behind schedule.

A SWISS spokesperson confirmed the incident happened, though noted that the takeoffs were aborted at a low speed of around 50 kilometers per hour (around 30 miles per hour).

What explains the aborted takeoffs? Well, it was because as the plane accelerated for takeoff, the automatic thrust control system automatically deactivated. To explain this as simply as possible, as I understand it, on the A220 when the auto-thrust is armed and the thrust levers are moved forward for takeoff, the auto-thrust then takes over, and moves the levers forward without manual intervention.

In other words, one of the pilots keeps their hands on the auto-thrust levers and “moves” with them, but doesn’t actually apply any force. Pilots are trained this way, and to not manually apply force. In the event that the crew tries to stop the auto-thrust lever motion, a pressure switch detects this, and then disengages the auto-thrust, to allow for a manual override.

In this case, the auto-thrust incorrectly detected resistance, when the pilots weren’t attempting to apply it. According to the airline, the system that monitors the aircraft’s technical status in real time was unable to identify the cause of the error, as no errors were displayed in the system. So at first, the pilots likely wondered if they had accidentally applied force.

However, once technicians had a look at the plane, it was discovered that the switch for disabling the automatic thrust control on the original aircraft was stuck, and this caused the automatic thrust control to shut down during takeoff attempts.

So while this can understandably seem scary to passengers, this wasn’t even a direct safety issue. After all, the pilots could’ve also manually moved the throttles. However, you also don’t want to take off when you know there’s an issue with the throttles, since that’s not exactly a best practice.

A SWISS Airbus A220 attempted a takeoff from Zurich three times in a row. While I’ve had two consecutive aborted takeoffs, I’ve never had three, and I can’t imagine that happens all too often.

While this is unusual, it sounds like this was handled well, and I can see why the pilots kept trying. This wasn’t a critical safety issue, but instead, just an incorrect detection of inputs, in a way that wouldn’t really pose a risk to the flight. At the same time, you don’t want to knowingly take off with a fault switch.

What do you make of this SWISS aborted takeoff trio?

#6182. Senate Dems dismiss talk of earlier leadership election; Schumer confident

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., leaves the Senate Democrats’ lunch meeting in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Democrats moved Tuesday to squelch talk of an accelerated timeline for the vote for a new majority leader, signaling they intend to keep the contest on Dec. 1.

That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.

The prospect of an earlier vote had been floated as a way to prevent internal divisions from hobbling the incoming majority before the 120th Congress even began.

But supporters of Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., both in the chamber and among party activists outside it, were increasingly casting the idea of a shorter contest as a bid to halt momentum for his bid against Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.

Even as Schumer maintained that he has the votes necessary to be elected as majority leader, several senators insisted Tuesday the discussion taking place within the caucus was a good thing.

“I’m confident I’ll be the next leader. I have the votes,” Schumer told reporters on Tuesday following the conference’s lunch.

Van Hollen for his part told reporters Tuesday he believes his bid has “momentum at this point in time, which is why there was an effort to short-circuit the process.”

“And fortunately, I think that will fail.”

Several senators leaving the meeting said the topic of the leadership contest did not come up at all, and that neither Van Hollen nor Schumer gave a presentation regarding their bids.

That was in large part due to the absence of the incoming senators — which could be as high as 13, depending on how the dust settles in Alaska — who are able to vote in the leadership elections. Retiring senators do not cast a ballot.

With such a large class of incoming freshman, several incumbents saw it crucial to keep the election scheduled as is.

“No one has ever raised that with me. I mean, I saw a rumor that some were wanting to contemplate that,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said Tuesday after the meeting. “The leadership discussions did not come up today. And part of the reason is we didn’t have the newcomers.”

“Remember, they all get a vote in the leadership discussion, and it would be hard to get them here,” Kaine continued, noting that only Sen.-elect Scott Colom, D-Miss., was present for Tuesday’s lunch amid his belated orientation. “But nobody else was here, and that discussion needs to have the newcomers because newcomers get votes. The outgoers don’t, right?”

Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. echoed that sentiment on Monday evening, saying, “I want to hear from the freshman class as well.”

Sen. Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, said, “I don’t know that” when asked about moving up the elections. “I think that we need to make sure that there’s enough time for what I would call a robust discussion about what we’re going to do. I think we should be very embracing of the new people who have been through fire to get here, and I think that we have to make sure that all these voices are heard.

“They’ve got a lot of talent to bring to the table,” she said.

Several senators-elect are among those who have publicly thrown their hats into Van Hollen’s corner, including Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan.El-Sayed on Tuesday said at The Atlantic Summit that he sees Van Hollen as “unique” in his experience in the Senate and running the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee as well as what he called “a willingness to take risks.”

“We need people who are willing to take legislative risk,” he said. “We need to rethink the way we legislate. It just should not be the process where you make one or two omnibus pieces of legislation that nobody really knows what’s in them,” he continued, advocating for piecemeal legislation.

But there are about 15 Democrats who have publicly backed Schumer’s bid. If former Rep. Mary Peltola maintains her lead in the lone outstanding Senate race in Alaska, Schumer would need 29 to secure the helm of the ship.

“I committed to Sen. Schumer literally months ago, and I continue to support him,” Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., said Monday. “I’m incredibly excited about the new ideas that our new colleagues have, and their energy, and the potential for changing the way we operate in the Senate, which we have to do because we need to be more effective.”

Several incumbents have also thrown their support behind Van Hollen for leadership change, including Sens. Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Bernie Sanders of Vermont.“I think, as I’ve said many times, the American people want change in the way we do business here in Washington, and I think Chris Van Hollen would be a great leader of the Democrats,” Sanders said Monday.

Several senators and senators-elect are refusing to comment publicly on who they’ll back.

That included Sen. Ben Ray Lujan, D-N.M., who said he wants “to hear the commitments from folks that are pursuing this leadership role as well as every leadership position in the Senate, as well as chairs of committees, to what their commitments are to having a strong agenda that’s going to improve people’s lives.”

Kaine is also in that camp, and insisted Monday he hadn’t made up his mind. But he did speak positively of Schumer’s recruiting efforts in the midterms and history of dealing with a Trump White House.

“Schumer just delivered a major win for us. No one who was not on the ballot worked harder for this victory than Chuck Schumer,” he said. “Chuck Schumer also happens to know Donald Trump better than anybody else in the caucus, and dealing with this wounded president is going to be a challenge over the next few years.”

“The voters are also overwhelmingly demanding change,” he said. “So we got to figure that out as a caucus, and we’re going to be able to. And we’re not afraid to have a discussion because we’re Democrats. We like democracy.”

Sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., also remained mum on who he’ll support but said, “You can’t argue” Schumer brought Democrats the majority.

“I think it’s a healthy thing to try and improve how the conference goes about its business,” he said. “I don’t think that is a distraction. We can deal with some distractions. We have to keep our eye on the ball.”

Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., who last week called for new leadership in a news conference with Sanders, days before Van Hollen’s announcement, was noncommittal arriving to the Capitol on Monday if that meant she’d be supporting the Maryland Democrat.

Senate Democrats’ election will most likely be a secret ballot. And most senators remained unified against moving the leadership elections before they recess for the Thanksgiving break.

“They should not be moved up. There was a reason that those rule changes took place before, and they should take place in December,” Lujan said.

Kaine dismissed Van Hollen’s challenge as anything unusual.

“We’re Democrats. It’s frankly unusual that there usually [aren’t] challenges to Democratic leaders because we’re Democrats,” he said. “It’s been a little unusual to have been here for 13 years and not really have them like this. But I think it’s a discussion not just about the two contenders for the leader role, but also the leadership team and priorities, and it’s all wrapped up in one discussion.”

“That’s why we decided, don’t do these votes until December, because you want to let the election settle and understand exactly what’s up, and then hear from potential votes.”

Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., said, “I think we should stick with the rules when it comes to the caucus. … That’s going to be what makes sure that we show that we have a real process.”

Sanders asked: “Why would anyone want to do that?” when asked.

“I think there’s a date that’s been called, and that should be the date.”

#6181. American Airlines Hasn’t Flown To Israel Since October 7—Now It’s Partnering With The Airline Flying Its Old Jets

American Airlines hasn’t flown to Israel since the October 7, 2023 attacks. Israir is flying the route using two of American’s retired Airbus A330s. Now American is partnering with Israir to connect those passengers to its network beyond New York. In August I flagged that Israir had acquired American’s old aircraft. Now it’s getting access to more of the customers it needs to fill those planes. American, meanwhile, gets connecting passengers and an Israeli sales partner ahead of its own planned return to the Israel market. Israir currently flies five times a week between New York JFK and Tel Aviv. American plans to resume daily service March 27, 2027, using Boeing 777-200ERs. I’d covered their previous plan to return in March 2026, they’ve kept planning to return and then not, given instability in the region even as other U.S. carriers flew. Ex-American Airlines Airbus A330-200 N287AY, Credit: Anna Zvereva / Wikimedia Commons. What American And Israir Have Agreed To The initial arrangement has two parts: Israir will put its flight code on American’s JFK–Tel Aviv service. Israir can market an American-operated flight as part of its own offering when American returns. An interline agreement will connect passengers beyond JFK. Travelers crossing the Atlantic on either airline will be able to combine that flight with American connections across the United States, Canada, Latin America and the Caribbean. An interline agreement supplies the framework for selling a connecting trip on one ticket and through-checking bags. A codeshare adds another airline’s flight number to the same flight. The initial codeshare involves Israir marketing American’s flight. American hasn’t announced that it’s putting its code on Israir’s A330 service. Israir’s stock exchange filing says the agreement was signed November 19, with initial implementation targeted by the end of 2026. That depends on regulatory approvals, technology and operational readiness. Israir Airbus A320, Credit: Oyoyoy via Wikimedia Commons Israir Sees A $20–40 Million Revenue Opportunity Until now, Israir’s New York route has competed primarily for passengers whose destination is New York. American connections let it compete for people going beyond New York as well. Israir estimates that this expands its potential customer market by 20–25%, creating an opportunity for $20–40 million in additional annual revenue. The filing though describes this as the larger addressable market rather than a revenue growth forecast. A codeshare on American’s flight also gives it something to sell when its own flight isn’t operating or its seats are full. For American, the near-term benefit is carrying Israir passengers on flights it’s already operating beyond JFK. Once American returns to Tel Aviv, Israir can also help sell seats on that flight through its own customer base and distribution in Israel. El Al And Delta Already Have A More Complete Partnership American is playing catch-up in Israel. Delta restored daily JFK–Tel Aviv service in September, and United returned that month as well. El Al and Arkia also serve the New York market. United can combine its Tel Aviv flying with its Newark hub. El Al has a Delta relationship that includes reciprocal codeshares, mileage earning and redemption, and elite benefits. That partnership began in 2024. What Passengers Get—And What They Don’t The immediate customer proposition is an easier connecting itinerary once the agreement goes live. Israir operates out of American’s JFK Terminal 8, so passengers won’t need to change terminals (and terminals aren’t connected airside at JFK). Passengers arriving from Israel still need to clear U.S. immigration and customs. Checking a bag through to the final destination doesn’t eliminate collecting and rechecking it on arrival in the United States. American also confirms Greenwich Lounge access at JFK for passengers flying Israir business class. However, there are no AAdvantage mileage earning, Loyalty Points, award redemptions or reciprocal elite benefits on Israir. The airlines say they’ll consider broader codesharing and AAdvantage benefits later. Hopefully status-earning and award redemption on Israir comes to fruition in the future. In August I flagged that Israir had acquired American’s old aircraft. Now it’s getting access to more of the customers it needs to fill those planes. American, meanwhile, gets connecting passengers and an Israeli sales partner ahead of its own planned return to the Israel market.

Israir currently flies five times a week between New York JFK and Tel Aviv. American plans to resume daily service March 27, 2027, using Boeing 777-200ERs. I’d covered their previous plan to return in March 2026, they’ve kept planning to return and then not, given instability in the region even as other U.S. carriers flew.

#6179. Mexico’s President Flew 21 Hours To China In Economy (In A Middle Seat!)

I’ve gotta say, huge kudos to Mexico’s President, Claudia Sheinbaum, for setting quite the example in terms of how she recently traveled to China, as flagged by View from the Wing…

World leaders have just met in Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders’ Meeting. As you’d expect, most leaders flew on their government planes. There were some exceptions, though I can’t imagine anyone else flew the same way as Mexico’s 64-year-old president.

Viajamos hacia Shenzhen para representar a México en el Foro de Cooperación Económica Asia-Pacífico (APEC) China 2026; la agenda de actividades incluye reunión con empresarios de países miembros. Además, participaré en la conferencia de prensa matutina para informar avances de… pic.twitter.com/F9UqRLjFlb

Media reports suggest she flew to China on China Southern. Specifically, she traveled on Sunday, November 15, 2026, on CZ8032, from Mexico City (MEX) to Shenzhen (SZX), with a refueling stop in Tijuana (TIJ), and the journey covering a distance of 8,803 miles.

The Airbus A350-900 took off from Mexico City at 12:49AM, arriving in Tijuana at 2:02AM, after a flight time of 3hr13min. Then it took off again at 4:34AM, and landed in Shenzhen the following morning at 11:31AM, after a flight time of 14hr56min. All-in-all, the flight took around 21 hours, including the refueling stop.

The shocking thing here isn’t that she traveled commercial, but instead, that she reportedly flew in economy! Reports suggest she was in seat 33B, which would be a middle seat in economy, no less!

Llegamos a la Ciudad de México en el vuelo CZ8031 desde Shenzhen, China. Agradecemos a toda la tripulación por su apoyo. pic.twitter.com/DSC83CpnDQ

I think a head of state should reasonably be able to fly business class on a flight of this length, for two reasons:

That being said, I absolutely commend her for the example she is setting. It’s certainly quite a contrast to what we’ve seen here, where President Trump accepted a Boeing 747-8 as a gift from Qatar, and talked about how he has done it to make Americans be proud, because “our country has to be represented properly.” Heck, just this week he talked about “China was very impressed” and “Russia was very impressed” of his new plane. Lovely, I’m happy we’re impressing Putin, that makes me proud to be an American!

"Russia was very impressed" — Trump leads his press conference by bragging about taking the longest flight in Air Force One history, in case you were worried that he actually accomplished something useful on his trip pic.twitter.com/dDIHg8wb1w

Keep in mind that Mexico has an interesting history when it comes to how leaders fly. In 2016, Mexico’s government took control of a private Boeing 787, which flew around former President Enrique Pena Nieto. The purchase of the plane had actually been arranged under the previous president, Felipe Calderón, in 2012.

Then in 2018, when Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador took charge in Mexico, he fulfilled a campaign promise of selling that 787, which turned out to be pretty challenging, given that demand for a secondhand VIP 787 isn’t exactly that high (the plane ended up going to Tajikistan). Sheinbaum has kept that general legacy going, by flying commercial.

Mexico’s President, Claudia Sheinbaum, traveled to the recent summit in China differently than virtually all other government leaders. Not only did she fly commercial, but she traveled in economy, and reportedly even in a middle seat.

There’s no denying that this is more about optics than anything, but I very much respect that. It’s nice to see heads of state who lead by example, as it’s pretty rare to see nowadays.

What do you make of Sheinbaum’s travel style?

Does China Southern offer wi-fi on its A350s? Hard to believe that the head of state of a country like Mexico would be out of reach for 21 hours.

Well, either she is a believer in living as the people do, or she’s a very smart politician whom knows humility is rare and appreciated these days… both options earn my praise.

Optics and propaganda. Waste of taxpayers money. For someone in her position, the biggest cost is "time". She should have been working with her cabinet members or other officials and also well rested for the meeting. A slip up could cost the country exports and percentage points in GDP. And it gets worse if she did work and used CZ wifi.

Every US airline CEO should be required to take a trip like this in the same seat once a year on a 12+ hour flight. Humble these arrogant pricks and make them experience the same dogshit product they offer their customers.

They could at least have given her an exit row seat! It shows how all the social media online hacks telling you how to get an upgrade are rubbish. If the President of Mexico isn’t getting an upgrade then what hope for anyone else.

The best cruise lines for families allow parents and kids to have fun together and apart while taking the stress out of group travel.

Our favorite family ships mix wow-factor activities with attractive kids clubs, plentiful and convenient dining and thoughtful touches like bathtubs and babysitting.

Your family might be happy anywhere there’s a beach or pool, but if you want an at-sea family vacation you’ll always remember, book a sailing with one of our top five cruise lines for families.

No one will be surprised that entertainment juggernaut Disney offers an amazing family cruise experience.

Disney Cruise Line ships are known for meet-and-greets with Mickey Mouse and Disney princesses, interactive movie-themed dining experiences and enormous kids clubs and play areas.

What might surprise the uninitiated is how good the line is at taking care of the whole family, not just the Mouse-obsessed little ones.

Disney thinks of all the little things that can help parents have a stress-free trip with kids in tow. From split bathrooms (allowing one family member to take a bath while another uses the toilet) to waiters who will cut up your child’s food, Disney Cruise Line takes the pressure off parents.

While other cruise lines limit water play to kids who are toilet trained and drop-off child care to ages 3 and up, Disney caters to all kids with onboard splash areas and nurseries for kids ages 6 months to 3 years.

Kids ages 3 to 10 live it up in the expansive Oceaneer Club, with attractions like an interactive replica of Star Wars’ Millennium Falcon and a play area designed to look like Andy’s Room from “Toy Story.”

Teens might roll their eyes at the ever-present Mickeys, but Disney Cruise Line does not ignore its older kid guests. Tweens and teens get their own cool hangouts, Edge (ages 11 to 14) and Vibe (ages 14 to 17), with video games, foosball and seating areas.

Additionally, first-run movies and Broadway-caliber musicals, waterslides, teen spa treatments and grab-and-go food options (and free room service) keep older kids busy and happy.

Sister ships Disney Wish, Disney Treasure and Disney Destiny feature Hero Zone sports areas for free play and competitions attractive to this age group. (Keep an eye out for the Disney Believe, too, debuting in late 2027.)

Grownups on Disney get to play as hard as they parent. Ships offer adults-only pool decks and restaurants, a nightlife scene and couples spa treatments to revive exhausted parents who haven't had a date in months.

The only caveat is that Disney Cruise Line is the most expensive cruise line on this list. At press time, seven-night Caribbean cruises start at $3,180 per person.

Related: These are the best cruise ships for kids

With some of the biggest ships at sea and an amusement park-like private island in the Bahamas, Royal Caribbean is one of the best cruise lines for active families.

Want to try surfing, sky diving, rock climbing, laser tag, bumper cars or zip lining? Families don’t have to leave the ship to find their adrenaline highs.

Even the sedentary pursuits are high-octane on Royal Caribbean. Broadway musicals, festive parades, water acrobatic performances and ice skating shows wow the crowds in the evenings and on sea days.

Expansive play spaces for kids includedrop-off nurseries for babies (ages 6 to 36 months) and Adventure Ocean for kids ages 3 to 12 (often broken into separate activities for kids ages 3 to 5, 6 to 8, and 9 to 12) with science labs and art studios on the biggest ships. Teens and tweens ages 13 to 17 get their own cool hangouts, often with activities scheduled around the ship.

While the kids live it up at cruise camp, parents can sneak off to the adults-only solarium or thermal suite.

After a hard day of play, worn-out families can refuel at a variety of restaurants, including burger and milkshake mecca Johnny Rockets, Italian and Mexican eateries and an all-day buffet.

Family cabins and connecting staterooms give larger families their needed space. The Ultimate Family Suite (and similar Ultimate Family Townhouses on some of the line’s biggest ships) can sleep eight to 10 people, and parents and kids alike might be tempted to stay up late playing air hockey, scrambling up the climbing wall, soaking in the private outdoor hot tub or watching the giant TV.

Royal Caribbean’s biggest ships – Icon, Star, and Legend of the Seas – also offers an entire section of the ship devoted to family-friendly accommodations and an outdoor dining-and-play space targeted at parents with young children.

Families should keep an eye out for kids-sail-free deals on select departures, which allow kids ages 12 and younger to pay no cruise fare when they sail as the third or fourth guest in a cabin with two full-fare-paying adults. (Note that families will still have to pay taxes, fees and port charges for kids sailing free.)

Fares for Royal Caribbean cruises can vary based on ship, and its newest, biggest ships often command premium pricing. Seven-night Caribbean cruises start from $444 per person on an older ship, but cost more than $1,000 per person on its biggest Icon Class ships.

Related: These are the best cruises for teens

Practicalities first: Carnival Cruise Line is an affordable and convenient cruise line for families who don’t live the jet-set lifestyle. With home ports all around the U.S., Carnival puts its ships within driving distance of many Americans.

A variety of short-cruise destinations, affordable-yet-spacious inside cabins (some that sleep up to four people) and lots of onboard attractions and restaurants included in the fares combine to make it one of the best value cruise lines afloat.

Carnival doesn’t dub its fleet the Fun Ships for nothing. The whole family will have a blast on board, whether you like getting down to live music, busting a gut at family-friendly comedy shows, being soaked at an onboard water park or eating green eggs and ham with Dr. Seuss characters.

The cruise line also embraces simple pleasures like free-flowing soft-serve ice cream and pizza and a day spent lounging by the pool.

Families don’t need to pull out their wallets to feed ravenous teens or sugar-fueled children. Guy Fieri burgers and barbecue, burritos for breakfast and lunch and Shaquille O’Neal’s fried chicken are all included in your cruise fares. No one’s going to make you dress up for dinner, either.

Carnival ships have plenty of cabins that can sleep four or five passengers, but six of its newerst ships truly treat families right. Book a Family Harbor cabin or suite on Vista or Excel Class ships and get access to a family lounge stocked with all the essentials — snacks and coffee, games, Wi-Fi, movies and a concierge to make bookings so mom and dad can spend more time playing with the kids.

Seven-night Caribbean cruises start at $443 per person.

It might not be a household name yet, but any cruise line that has a partnership with Lego should be on every family’s radar,  so MSC Cruises is a line families should know.

As the Mediterranean line grows its U.S.-based fleet, it's adding newer and bigger family-friendly ships to more home ports, including Miami, Port Canaveral, Galveston and Seattle.

MSC World America, the line’s newest and biggest ship sailing the Caribbean, features the Family Aventura district, a hub for kids and their grownups. It features The Harbour, an outdoor space with a ropes course, waterpark, playground and 11-deck-long dry slide; indoor sports area for family games and bumper cars; and an enormous Doremiland kids club.

Speaking of kids clubs, MSC’s ships offer play spaces for babies, kids, tweens and teens. Its ships not only offer a drop-off Baby Club (ages 6 months to 3 years) with educational toys by Chicco but also a special baby laundry service to take care of that pile of dirty onesies.

MSC divides young cruisers into Mini Club (ages 3 to 6), Junior Club (ages 7 to 11) and Young Club (12 to 14). Kids club activities go beyond arts and crafts and video games to include cooking events, sports competitions and high-tech interactive games. Teens (ages 15 to 17) can sing karaoke, dance at the onboard disco and attend themed parties with their new friends.

Outside of the kids club, families can race in a Formula One simulator, experience virtual reality, be soaked in a water park or brave their fear of heights on a suspension bridge.

Several MSC Cruises ships offer thrill rides that will appeal to all ages of adventurous cruisers. MSC Seascape features Robotron, a three-seat robotic amusement ride and MSC World America and MSC World Atlantic (coming late 2027) have the Cliffhanger, an overwater swing ride – both are hits with thrill-seeking families.

Multigenerational groups can choose connecting cabins for more space, but families keen on rooming together can take advantage of frequent "kids sail free" fares and pay only the taxes and fees for children under 18 who are the third and fourth passengers in a cabin. Seven-night Caribbean cruises start from $299 per person.

Norwegian Cruise Line is all about giving cruisers options to create different versions of the perfect cruise vacation, all within the same ship.

The flexibility and choice make it one of the best cruise lines for families, especially those who need to satisfy diverse interests or who are easily bored with the same activities day after day.

Kids clubs and adults-only sundecks allow for age-appropriate fun time apart, but Norwegian wants families to have fun together. Its Splash Academy engages kids ages 3 to 12 with group activities like team challenges and crafts, while Entourage is the place for teens ages 13 to 17 to make friends, hang out playing foosball and video games or show off their moves during evening dance parties. Adults can hide out in the 18+ Vibe Beach Club and Spice H2O for some sunbathing and hot tub time while the kids are engaged in youth activities.

Norwegian also wants families to have fun together. Teaming up to solve a murder mystery, mastering a ropes course, singing along to a high-energy musical show or live concert or screaming down a waterslide are guaranteed to create those unbreakable family bonds.

Norwegian’s flexible dining system and a plethora of onboard eateries let families plan meals to suit their schedules and tastes.

Also, free kids meals at extra-charge restaurants mean parents can sample Brazilian, Japanese, French or seafood dishes while the littles gobble up pasta and chicken fingers. Casual all-day options suit fussy eaters who need unfussy dining areas.

The cruise line also gets a shoutout for its family-friendly Hawaii itineraries. As the only big-ship cruise line that sails weeklong itineraries round trip from Honolulu, Norwegian provides an easy way for families to visit multiple islands.

Beach time, boat rides, water sports, luaus and volcano tours combine for an epic family trip, with the ship taking the stress out of meals and transportation.

In the Bahamas, Norwegian’s enhanced Great Stirrup Cay private island now features a waterpark with a variety of slides, a cliff jump and a not-that-lazy river (entrance fee required), as well as free use of a giant pool and a splash playground for little kids, making beach days even more fun for vacationing families.

To make it all more affordable, families should keep an eye on Norwegian’s Free at Sea promotion, which sometimes includes free third and fourth guest fares. That means that kids sharing a room with two paying adults sail free. Fares for seven-night Caribbean cruises start at $399 per person.

Families can have a great time on almost any cruise line, hanging out by the pool, visiting exciting new destinations and simply spending time together. But if you’re looking for a ship that really caters to kids and their adult companions, you’ll want to book a vacation with one of these five best cruise lines for families.

#6177. American Airlines Says Operations Chief David Seymour Will Retire — With Dismissal-Style Severance

American Airlines chief operating officer David Seymour is leaving the job December 31. CEO Robert Isom calls it a retirement. The agreement American signed with Seymour gives him severance on terms normally reserved for dismissal without cause or resignation for good reason. American’s last proxy put the cash severance alone at $2,750,625 for a hypothetical departure on December 31, 2025, with total value over $7 million. The airline hasn’t disclosed the final amount for this exit. [T]he Company will provide Mr. Seymour with the severance payments and benefits pursuant to the covered termination provisions set forth in his previously disclosed Severance Agreement with the Company dated as of September 20, 2023

[T]he Company will provide Mr. Seymour with the severance payments and benefits pursuant to the covered termination provisions set forth in his previously disclosed Severance Agreement with the Company dated as of September 20, 2023

JonCarlo “JC” Gulbranson takes over January 1, reporting directly to Isom. He’s the executive I flagged as Seymour’s likely successor in August, when American handed him much of the job.

Aviation watchdog JonNYC shared Isom’s message to employees. Isom thanks Seymour for his friendship and his work bringing US Airways and American together. Before joining America West in 1999, Seymour led a platoon in the 82nd Airborne. Just last month he went back to West Point and Fort Bragg with Medal of Honor recipients to meet the cadets and soldiers who followed him there.

AA pic.twitter.com/9919XVOKrW — JonNYC (@xJonNYC) November 20, 2026

Under Seymour’s contract, cash severance is 18 months of salary plus a year and a half of target bonus. He also gets money for 18 months of health premiums, and his stock can keep vesting during those 18 months. Between cash, stock, health premiums and flight benefits he’d already earned, American’s illustration in its latest proxy came to $7.13 million. Separately, Seymour remains eligible for his 2026 annual bonus. His advisory job pays $25,000 a month for up to three months ($75,000), plus executive benefits. His contract calculates severance using pay immediately before termination. Seymour has to sign a release and honor his existing restrictions, and American says it’ll file the full transition letter with its annual report. Those flight benefits include lifetime confirmed personal travel in any cabin for Seymour and his immediate family, Admirals Club access and another 12 confirmed roundtrips a year for friends and other relatives. The Handoff Started In August When American put Heather Garboden in charge of the customer experience, they gave her two bosses. She was supposed to persuade customers to pay more to fly American while reporting both to commercial and to the executive responsible for getting flights off the gate on time. When a pilot asked Seymour in 2022 what American was doing about poor customer satisfaction, his answer was “I think we’re on a good path to get there.” He went on to talk about running the operation. What was Garboden supposed to do when the catering truck was late and the choice was a delayed departure or six hours in first class without meals? In August Garboden began reporting solely to chief commercial officer Nat Pieper and picked up catering, reservations and service recovery. Pieper also got marketing, brand, advertising and partnerships as American broke up Global Engagement head Ron DeFeo’s group. Caroline Clayton took corporate communications. Then I reported network chief Brian Znotins was leaving as Pieper set out to rebuild flying in big cities where American had pulled back. Seymour actually picked up American Eagle in August. But Gulbranson got the airports and operations planning on top of flight operations, flight attendants and the control center. Now he gets safety, regulatory compliance and aircraft maintenance, too. Corporate security goes to government affairs chief Steve Neuman. American will tell employees in December who gets the regionals. If this hadn’t actually been decided already, then August was Gulbranson’s audition. Isom’s memo introduces the retirement as the next step in the August reorganization. Seymour’s contract even lists a material reduction in responsibilities as grounds that can qualify an executive for severance. We don’t know who first proposed retirement, but this looks to me like a negotiated handoff that was already well underway. American Had To Retrofit Planes It Had Just Retrofitted While there are numerous stories like it – such as insufficient oversight of outsourced Maintenance, Repair, and Overhaul – I always think of a few things about Seymour’s tenure. One is explaining why the airline wouldn’t invest in RFID baggage tags like Delta despite perpetually bottom of the industry performance in mishandled bags. Another is failing to fix ‘Concept D’ business class seats that rocked. And the biggest is mismanaging cabin retrofits of the domestic fleet. Seymour was running integrated operations when the first American Airlines 737 MAX introduced the cabin that would go into its existing 737s and Airbus A321s. A flight attendant eventually asked whether anyone had built a mockup before committing to it. They hadn’t. Doug Parker said network planning had largely driven the design. Seymour called it “a mistake that should not have happened” and later explained what American had changed. For subsequent cabins they’d bring in real seats, build overhead bins and try pushing a service cart through. In his words, “We do mockups and not just you know ‘tape it out.’” Flight attendants working in the back galley had to help passengers get out of the lavatories because the two doors opened into each other and caught. The sinks were too shallow for the water pressure. I washed my hands on the inaugural flight and got water all over my shirt and pants, as did everyone else. Up front, the seat supports took up the space where a first class passenger was supposed to put a bag. American was still installing the interior after deciding to fix it. Project Oasis put the new seats into existing 737s. Then Project Kodiak went back into planes they’d already redone to fix the storage, give the first row some legroom back and add the device holders coach passengers already had. How Well Did American Actually Run? After the troubled summer of 2019, American gave Seymour responsibility for all operations. The following June he got the chief operating officer title and added flight service. For years my frustration was that when the operation fell short, the answer seemed to be to give the executive running it a bigger job. In 2023 American completed its highest share of scheduled flights since the merger and edged out United on domestic on-time arrivals. And spreading the Dallas schedule from nine daily rushes to 13 smaller ones helped passengers this year. The hub chief reported half as many missed connections in the first 17 days. But by 2025 American ranked eighth of ten network airlines for on-time arrivals. And the Transportation Department’s new figures show that Delta and United both beat American every single month from January through September 2026. Counting domestic flights including regional partners, American came in at 73.30% on time, United at 76.20% and Delta at 78.31%. American canceled 46,059 flights, or 2.99% of its schedule, against 1.75% at United and 2.25% at Delta. Credit: American Airlines One clue to what management valued is in that same proxy. In August 2025 the board gave Seymour a retention stock award worth about $2 million at target. The entire award turns on avoiding cancellations American counts as controllable. A flight that runs three hours late still counts as a success on that measure. The award measures performance through June 2027, so it can still pay out after he’s gone. Gulbranson is well regarded inside American. He started at Northwest, joined US Airways in 2008 and helped integrate flight operations systems during the merger. He’s run both the control center that decides what to cancel and the customer care operation that hears from the people who get stranded. Credit: American Airlines Listen to the two men describe January’s Winter Storm Fern. Seymour said the technology worked as intended and that he hadn’t seen reports of flight attendants sleeping in airports even as his boss Isom acknowledged crew had slept on floors. Gulbranson went before the pilots’ union board and told them where management had misjudged the storm and overestimated how quickly they could recover. The union’s account called his assessment “unvarnished.” That’s one reason I’m glad he’ll be running the operation the next time it snows in Dallas and up the East Coast. #6176. Why JSX Just Bought New Pacific Airlines, The Strange, Failed 757 Startup

Public charter air carrier JSX has just acquired New Pacific Airlines, and with this, New Pacific Airlines intends to resume flights, with Embraer E145 aircraft.

If you’re not familiar with New Pacific Airlines, you’re probably thinking “huh?” If you are familiar with New Pacific Airlines, you’re probably thinking “WTF?” There’s a sneaky and logical explanation here, so let me explain.

Let’s start with a little context. JSX is a public charter air carrier, which operates a fleet of nearly 60 planes, most of which are Embraer E135s and E145s.

It operates as a Part 135 operator, meaning it’s not technically an airline, as it’s using a loophole that allows it to not use standard TSA security screening, hire pilots with fewer than 1,500 hours, etc. Basically what’s happening is that one subsidiary sells the tickets, and then another subsidiary operates the flights, so it’s technically a “charter” (with 30 people who don’t know one another).

Then there’s New Pacific Airlines, one of the strangest airline startups we’ve ever seen, and which I’ve covered extensively. The airline acquired some Boeing 757s, and the business plan was to connect North America and Asia via Anchorage (ANC).

The business model made zero sense in the first place, though there was some funding there, and they even invested in constructing a lounge in Anchorage, even though those flights never did happen. The airline did briefly fly from (ONT) to Nashville (BNA) — as one does — before ultimately going out of business.

That brings us to the news. New Pacific Airlines intends to resume flights with Embraer E145s that are leased from JSX, as reported by IshrionA. According to a Department of Transportation filing, the airline intends to resume flights with planes featuring 42 seats, which is higher than the 30-seat limit you’ll find on current JSX planes.

JSX acquires New Pacific Airlines.New Pacific Airlines intends to resume flights with ERJ 145 leased from JSX. pic.twitter.com/uMMS0J2fZy

On the surface, this of course makes absolutely no sense. New Pacific Airlines was out of business, and the business model made no sense. So why would JSX buy an airline and then lease planes to it?

Long story short, this seems to be a play to acquire a cheap Part 121 certificate. A Part 121 operator is a company that’s allowed to operate scheduled air transport… in other words, a “real” airline. As I mentioned above, JSX has historically been a Part 135 operator, and that explicitly means it’s not an airline. It’s a public charter air carrier, so it’s not a “real” airline.

Going back a couple of years, we know that the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) was considering cracking down on carriers like JSX, since they definitely don’t operate within the spirit of the rules. That’s not to say that JSX did anything wrong, because by the letter of the law, they’re following it exactly. It’s just that the letter of the law makes no sense, and clearly doesn’t reflect the intent behind distinguishing between Part 121 and Part 135 operators.

Under Trump, there was no scrutiny of this. However, with Democrats soon controlling both the House and Senate, I imagine JSX leaders may be worried that there could again be more scrutiny. If nothing else, buying a cheap Part 121 certificate is a good insurance policy, in case the government does crack down. After all, these can basically be “sold,” while acquiring one from scratch can be grueling process.

I wouldn’t assume that anything will really operate with New Pacific Airlines branding, or based on a New Pacific Airlines business model. Instead, I imagine the idea is that JSX will start dabbling in Part 121 operations, which is why these planes will have more seats (above the 30-seat cap that’s allowed), since that’s no longer a factor.

If the government were to crack down on Part 135 operators, JSX could move to Part 121 operations. However, they’d have to make lots of changes, from their pilot hiring, to the way passengers are screened.

JSX has just bought New Pacific, the airline with an absurd business model that went bankrupt. No, JSX isn’t inspired by the concept of flying Boeing 757s to Asia. Instead, this is clearly the cheapest way for JSX to acquire a Part 121 certificate, which would be required for the carrier to continue operations in the event that the government were to crack down on the Part 135 operator loophole.

It’s going to be interesting to see how this evolves, both since JSX seems to have plans to operate Part 121 operations in the near future, and also to see how JSX’s business model would evolve if the Part 135 concept were blocked.

What do you make of this JSX Part 121 play?

#6175. Buy Southwest Rapid Rewards Points For 50% Off (1.5 Cents Each): Worth It?

Looking to buy Southwest points? Rapid Rewards is currently offering up to a 50% discount on purchased points, which is an opportunity to acquire them for just 1.5 cents each. Is that a good deal?

While there has long been value in strategically buying points, the concept of a revenue based frequent flyer program selling points can be tougher to rationalize. So that I don’t bury the lede, let me say that I’d only buy points in a very narrow set of circumstances, like if trying to top off a points balance for a specific redemption.

Link: Buy Southwest Rapid Rewards points with this promotion for 50% off

Between 12:01AM CT on November 19 and 11:59PM CT on December 31, 2026, Southwest Rapid Rewards is offering a discount on purchased points. With Southwest, it’s common for different members to be eligible for different offers, so you’ll have to log into your Rapid Rewards account to see what you’re eligible for.

However, the best version of the offer to buy Southwest points provides up to a 50% discount, structured as follows:

Ordinarily you can buy Southwest points for 3.0 cents each, and that price is inclusive of the 7.5% federal excise tax. Given the limit of being able to purchase up to 100,000 Rapid Rewards points per day, that means if you maxed out this promotion, you could buy 100,000 points for $1,500, which is a cost of 1.5 cents per point.

Southwest sells points in increments of 1,000 points, with 2,000 points being the minimum. Ordinarily there’s a daily maximum of buying 60,000 points, but during this promotion, that cap has been increased to 100,000 points.

Just in the interest of being thorough, some Rapid Rewards members may be eligible for smaller percentage discounts, so let me crunch the numbers on those potential offers:

Southwest has no annual limit on how many Rapid Rewards points you can buy. The only restriction is that you can ordinarily buy at most 60,000 points per calendar day. During this promotion, that cap has been increased to 100,000 points, though.

Note that the purchase of Southwest points is non-refundable, and buying Southwest points doesn’t count toward Rapid Rewards elite status or Companion Pass qualification. Purchased points typically post nearly instantly, but in some cases, it can take up to 72 hours for them to post.

Southwest Rapid Rewards frequently offers promotions on purchasing points. When the program does have a buy points promotion, the 50% discount offer is pretty standard. So I’d recommend buying points based on when you have a relatively immediate use for redeeming them, rather than anything else.

Below is a chart with some of the recent Southwest buy points promotions that we’ve seen, before this one.

If you’d like to buy Southwest Airlines points, note that purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as an airfare purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. Therefore this wouldn’t be treated as a Southwest purchase if you’re using a Rapid Rewards credit card.

I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. See this post for more on which credit cards are best for buying points.

Southwest Rapid Rewards is a revenue based frequent flyer program, and the number of points required for a flight is roughly correlated to the revenue cost of a flight. However, there is a dynamic element to the pricing, whereby the value you get per point varies significantly, based on the flight and fare class you redeem for. With this, we’re seeing redemption values as low as 1.1 cents per point, and as high as 1.5 cents per point, give or take.

As you can tell, there are probably few situations where it makes sense to buy points for 1.5 cents (or more) each, when they can’t be redeemed for that, best case scenario.

Let me cut to the chase — there are few situations where it makes sense to purchase Rapid Rewards points. Even at the discounted cost, there’s not usually value in buying points for 1.5 cents each when you can typically only redeem them for less than that. So don’t buy these points speculatively, unless you know exactly what you’re doing, and have a redemption in mind.

There are three potential scenarios I’d like to address, including the main scenario where I think it could make sense (but not really), which is to build up a balance of Southwest points, given the flexibility this provides.

Some might buy Rapid Rewards points in order to top off their account so they have enough points for a Rapid Rewards award ticket. I guess this might be worth it to some if you need a small number of points, though personally I’d just keep collecting points and then redeem with your next ticket.

The Southwest Airlines Companion Pass is one of the best values in domestic travel. If you qualify for this, you can always have a companion travel with you for just the standard taxes, regardless of whether you’re booking a cash ticket or redeeming points.

For those with a Companion Pass, buying Southwest points could get you outsized value:

However, there’s still absolutely zero reason to do that. You’d be better off just booking a paid ticket and then having a companion fly with you.

There is one major benefit in general to paying for a ticket with Southwest Rapid Rewards points rather than cash. While Southwest Airlines has no change fees on both revenue and award tickets on most kinds of fares:

I do think there’s big value in having a stash of Rapid Rewards points. I use this when I speculatively want to book travel (including for friends and family), since there’s no downside.

If you’re looking to earn Southwest points, there are plenty of ways to rack up this currency with credit card rewards:

On top of that, Rapid Rewards has a variety of co-branded Chase credit cards, which can be a great way to rack up rewards. This includes cards like the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card (learn more), Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Performance Business Credit Card (learn more), etc.

Through December 31, 2026, Southwest is selling Rapid Rewards points with a discount of up to 50%, which brings the cost down to as little as 1.5 cents per point. I still don’t think there are many circumstances under which it makes sense to buy points, given that Rapid Rewards is a revenue based frequent flyer program, and points can typically only be redeemed for 1.1-1.5 cents each toward the cost of a ticket.

Under what circumstances do you think it’s worth buying Southwest Airlines points?

#6174. Denver Airport’s $225,000 Lawyer Has Been Paid To Stay Home For 8 Months—The City Wants Permission To Fire Him

Denver airport’s top lawyer has spent eight months on paid leave, collecting a salary of roughly $225,000 a year. Now Denver wants a federal judge to let it fire him. But the airport’s general counsel Everett Martinez says city officials retaliated against him for raising legal objections to their improper dealings and for refusing to help push out airport CEO Phil Washington. The city says he violated his professional obligations and wants to stop paying someone who can’t perform the job. Meanwhile, Denver has authorized up to $970,000 for outside lawyers handling his case and a separate employment lawsuit. The $470,000 budget for the first phase of his case is quite an expense for a fight between the city and its own airport lawyer. I’ve called Denver the worst airport in the country. It can work reasonably well as a connecting hub. Actually getting to and from Denver, through the terminal and out to a gate is another matter. This latest fight brings together several of the reasons the place inspires so little confidence: political interference, weak financial oversight, and executives spending their time fighting each other. The city’s November 10 filing argues keeping Martinez on leave is harming Denver during a budget crisis. Martinez wants paid leave to continue while he litigates, potentially for years. At approximately $225,000 annually, eight months works out to about $150,000 in salary, before benefits. That’s arithmetic, rather than a payroll accounting. The distinction between airport money and city money matters here. His salary is airport money. Martinez’s complaint says it comes entirely from the airport’s enterprise fund. That’s separate from Denver’s general fund. Airport revenue consists of things like airline rents and landing fees, parking and concession. That’s not money that can get moved to the city’s programs anyway. The outside defense contract is budgeted to city money. The council’s contract worksheet identifies the general fund as its funding source. So it’s actually the city that’s draining funds amidst a budget crisis, although it’s possible they try to bill it back to the airport. The $970,000 covers two cases. The city’s budget presentation allocates $470,000 to the first phase of Martinez’s case and $500,000 to a separate case. They’re authorizing spending ‘up to’ this amount at this stage. The amended agreement sets rates of $800 an hour for attorneys and $375 for paralegals. The firm is Wheeler Trigg O’Donnell, where city attorney Miko Brown previously worked. Funny that. Brown says a five-person panel considered four firms and unanimously selected this one, which Denver had used since 2011. She says she cast her vote for her former firm last. Martinez alleges he was punished after objecting to the Park Hill Golf Course land swap, warning against withholding information from federal aviation officials, and resisting pressure to help remove Washington. He also alleges discriminatory treatment and an ugly remark from Brown suggesting he get a noose. The city denies his allegations. The city didn’t want to lease airport space to a carrier involved in ICE deportation flights and Martinez wasn’t helpful in covering this up (it’s against the law). I coverde the Key Lime Air affair last year. Then I covered a memo supporting Martinez’s account that officials subsequently sought to manufacture a safety justification for the decision. The memo was written before his lawsuit, and another airport executive endorsed its accuracy. The Federal Aviation Administration opened a formal investigation into the lease denial with $90 million in federal grants at risk. Additionally, the city wanted airport property for a park. There are federal restrictions involved in transferrin ghte land. Martinez appears to have stood in the way (likely as he was obligated to). But the city has counterclaimed for breach of fiduciary duty, conversion and civil theft. Martinez may have a legitimate employment claim but that doesn’t give him the right to remain on the payroll throughout the litigation. He says his first amendment rights are being violated, but the Supreme Court generally doesn’t treat speech made pursuant to an employee’s official duties as protected citizen speech and giving the city legal advice was his job. And while he ostensibly also helped protect then-airport CEO Phil Washington, it’s not at all clear that Washington was doing a good job. (He retired August 1.) I covered Washington’s nomination to lead the Federal Aviation Administration and its collapse. He’d spent less than two years running an airport after a career in the military and public transit. During his confirmation hearing, he couldn’t answer a series of seven aviation questions from Senator Ted Budd. And his actual airport record is spotty. Construction oversight. A 2023 audit of the Great Hall project identified inadequate contractor oversight, procurement concerns and overcharges. The January 2025 follow-up found only two of ten recommendations for improvement fully implemented, and no corrective action on seven items. The construction debacle predated Washington, but I view his record as overall quite bad on accountability. Concession revenue. After an audit found weaknesses in rent collection and monitoring concessionaire deductions, the airport accepted 13 recommendations. By October 2025, only three were fully implemented. Accounting problems continued. Executive travel. I wrote about the extraordinary airfare bills for a Madrid conference. The ethics board’s written decision lists $12,047.01 for Washington’s airfare and $19,194.21 for his chief operating officer. My hunch is they were running for MileagePlus status. The board dismissed the ethics complaint for insufficient evidence of private gain, while sharply criticizing the spending and Washington’s response. His ‘need to be ready-to-work-on-arrival’ justification looked weak when he arrived three days before being on the program. The trains remain a good illustration of the airport’s deeper problem. I covered 131 breakdowns over a year. Most interruptions were brief. But passengers still lack a walking alternative to the B and C concourses. Denver is finally planning pedestrian routes through existing baggage tunnels, estimated at $300 million to $700 million, with completion expected in 2028 or 2029. That’s where I’d like to see the airport’s management attention go. Instead, airport users are paying a sidelined general counsel, city taxpayers are funding the defense against him, and the people responsible for running the place are arguing over whether their own lawyer can be trusted.
