But the airport’s general counsel Everett Martinez says city officials retaliated against him for raising legal objections to their improper dealings and for refusing to help push out airport CEO Phil Washington. The city says he violated his professional obligations and wants to stop paying someone who can’t perform the job.

Meanwhile, Denver has authorized up to $970,000 for outside lawyers handling his case and a separate employment lawsuit. The $470,000 budget for the first phase of his case is quite an expense for a fight between the city and its own airport lawyer.

I’ve called Denver the worst airport in the country. It can work reasonably well as a connecting hub. Actually getting to and from Denver, through the terminal and out to a gate is another matter. This latest fight brings together several of the reasons the place inspires so little confidence: political interference, weak financial oversight, and executives spending their time fighting each other.

The city’s November 10 filing argues keeping Martinez on leave is harming Denver during a budget crisis. Martinez wants paid leave to continue while he litigates, potentially for years. At approximately $225,000 annually, eight months works out to about $150,000 in salary, before benefits. That’s arithmetic, rather than a payroll accounting.

The distinction between airport money and city money matters here.

The outside defense contract is budgeted to city money. The council’s contract worksheet identifies the general fund as its funding source. So it’s actually the city that’s draining funds amidst a budget crisis, although it’s possible they try to bill it back to the airport.

The $970,000 covers two cases. The city’s budget presentation allocates $470,000 to the first phase of Martinez’s case and $500,000 to a separate case. They’re authorizing spending ‘up to’ this amount at this stage.

The amended agreement sets rates of $800 an hour for attorneys and $375 for paralegals. The firm is Wheeler Trigg O’Donnell, where city attorney Miko Brown previously worked. Funny that. Brown says a five-person panel considered four firms and unanimously selected this one, which Denver had used since 2011. She says she cast her vote for her former firm last.

Martinez alleges he was punished after objecting to the Park Hill Golf Course land swap, warning against withholding information from federal aviation officials, and resisting pressure to help remove Washington. He also alleges discriminatory treatment and an ugly remark from Brown suggesting he get a noose. The city denies his allegations.

The city didn’t want to lease airport space to a carrier involved in ICE deportation flights and Martinez wasn’t helpful in covering this up (it’s against the law). I coverde the Key Lime Air affair last year.

Then I covered a memo supporting Martinez’s account that officials subsequently sought to manufacture a safety justification for the decision. The memo was written before his lawsuit, and another airport executive endorsed its accuracy. The Federal Aviation Administration opened a formal investigation into the lease denial with $90 million in federal grants at risk.

Additionally, the city wanted airport property for a park. There are federal restrictions involved in transferrin ghte land. Martinez appears to have stood in the way (likely as he was obligated to).

But the city has counterclaimed for breach of fiduciary duty, conversion and civil theft. Martinez may have a legitimate employment claim but that doesn’t give him the right to remain on the payroll throughout the litigation. He says his first amendment rights are being violated, but the Supreme Court generally doesn’t treat speech made pursuant to an employee’s official duties as protected citizen speech and giving the city legal advice was his job. As someone who deals with public entity employment liability issues, this case is tough for sure but has little to do with the fiscal crisis there which is poor management and poor spending priorities of the taxpayers funds. It also has little to do with the poor airport layout or bad planning that went into this ‘temple of doom’ money pit.

If the city fires him and then loses the case they may still owe him for back pay anyway, in addition to his legal fees and benefits. Whistleblower protections are strong for employees even if the guy is not a good employee. If he was to also win punitive damages it could be much more and the jury pool in that area might just give him a nuclear verdict in a case like this since they would just look at the city and airport authority as a ‘Daddy War-bucks’, having unlimited money and ‘big pockets’ in the form of insurance policies that also would contribute. This, in turn could also lead to much higher premiums later. Denver is self insured on employment liability but a loss like that would get into their layers of excess insurance. They already pay over $15 million a year in premiums in addition to the heavy expenses of being mostly self insured for work comp, liability, etc.

What the city/airport should do is settle this through mediation asap and figure that spending $500k, $1 million, etc is better than spending $5+ million later. Well, that and do a better job of hiring which I doubt they do like most public entities that I know.

#6173. Mary Peltola unseats Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska

Former Alaska Rep. Mary Peltola speaks during her election night party in Anchorage on Nov. 3. (Charly Triballeau/ AFP via Getty Images)

Former Rep. Mary Peltola has defeated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, giving Senate Democrats their ninth pickup of the midterm elections and bringing their caucus’s total seats in the next Congress to 56.

The Associated Press called the race for Peltola around 10:19 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday, a full two weeks after Election Day. The latest tranche of ballots counted put the former congresswoman past the 50-percent threshold to win the election outright without Alaska’s ranked choice voting system kicking in.

With her victory, Peltola, who is Yup’ik, becomes one of the first Native American women elected to the Senate, along with fellow Democrat Peggy Flanagan, who won the open seat in Minnesota this month.

“As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first.,” Peltola said in a statement after the race was called.

The Alaska race was the final Senate contest to be called in a midterm election that saw Democrats win commanding majorities in both chambers of Congress. Besides Alaska, Democrats also flipped Senate seats in North Carolina, Maine, Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi.

Peltola, a former state legislator, made history in 2022 when she became the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, winning a special election for the state’s at-large district. She comfortably won the general election that fall but was narrowly unseated in 2024 by Republican Nick Begich.

She entered the Senate contest in January, positioning herself as an independent-minded Democrat and invoking the legacies of two well-liked Alaska Republicans, the late Sen. Ted Stevens and the late Rep. Don Young, whom she succeeded in the House.

She campaigned on the slogan “fish, family, freedom” and played up her moderate views and deep roots in the state.

But the race was marked by allegations of political gamesmanship. In addition to the incumbent Sullivan, a retired colonel in the U.S. Marine Corps Reserves, the Senate ballot also included a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan. The New York Times reported late last month that operatives aligned with Peltola’s campaign were involved in the effort to recruit the second Dan Sullivan in an attempt to confuse voters.

Peltola has said she had no connection to the scheme.

Prior to Election Day, the Trump administration filed a lawsuit seeking to delay certification of the result if Sen. Sullivan were to lose. The lawsuit was tossed earlier this month by a federal judge.

Trump also suggested that all votes cast for Dan J. Sullivan should be added to the incumbent’s total. “If you add them up, Dan Sullivan wins,” the president told reporters Monday. But as of Tuesday evening when the race was called, Peltola had more votes than both Sullivans combined.

The Alaska race was initially viewed as a long shot for Democrats. The Last Frontier has elected a Democratic senator just once in the past 50 years – in 2008, when Mark Begich ousted Stevens. Begich, the Democratic uncle of the current Republican congressman, served a single term before he was ousted by Sullivan in 2014.

But anger in Alaska over the rising cost of food and fuel — already among the highest in the nation — provided Democrats with an opening.

"56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago," Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer said in a statement Tuesday night. "But I knew if we concentrated on getting the best candidates, and if we focused like a laser on the costs, corruption, and chaos that Donald Trump has wrought throughout America, we would have shot."

In other Alaska races, Democrats flipped the governor’s mansion, with former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins winning an open-seat race to become the first Democrat elected governor of the state since Tony Knowles won a second term in 1998.

The race for the state’s at-large House district will be decided by ranked choice voting, with tabulations expected to take place Wednesday. Begich, the GOP incumbent, was leading Tuesday with 47.5 percent of the vote and is expected to prevail over independent Bill Hill, who had the backing of national Democrats and trailed with 42 percent. Another Democrat and a Libertarian combined for the remainder of the vote.

The is a cobranded airline card for Atmos Rewards, the joint loyalty program for Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines. The card earns Atmos Rewards points, which TPG's November 2026 valuations place at 1.6 cents apiece — one of the highest airline currency valuations.

Its headline perk is an annual 25,000-point Global Companion Award, but its suite of benefits also includes a free first checked bag and preferred boarding (when you purchase your Alaska or Hawaiian flight with your card).

Cardholders also have a faster path to Atmos Rewards elite status, as they earn 1 status point for every $2 spent (with no spending cap) and receive an anniversary status points boost.

One of my favorite card perks is the Atmos Rewards Summit's standout earning rates, which are especially impressive compared to other airline cobranded cards. Cardholders earn 3 points per dollar spent on all foreign transactions, an unusual (and potentially quite rewarding) bonus category.

One of the best ways to redeem Atmos Rewards points is for flights on Alaska, Hawaiian, Oneworld and other partner airlines.

You'll generally get the most value by using your Atmos points for award flights.

#6170. Amex Blue Cash Preferred Review: A Top Cash Back Card For Everyday Purchases

If you spend a lot at supermarkets and want to earn cash back, the Blue Cash Preferred® Card from American Express is hard to beat. The card offers 6% cash back at U.S. supermarkets and on select streaming subscriptions, which can add up fast for families and anyone with a few monthly subscriptions.

In this post, I’ll cover the welcome offer, the bonus categories and how they work, the Disney streaming credit, and how this card compares to other options like the no annual fee Blue Cash Everyday® Card from American Express and the Citi Strata Premier® Card.

Link: Learn more about the Blue Cash Preferred® Card from American Express

Before I get into the Amex Blue Cash Preferred Card review, here’s a quick look at the most important features and fees:

And here are my thoughts on the main pros and cons of the Blue Cash Preferred Card:

When applying for a credit card, obviously the welcome offer, the eligibility, and the fees, are major considerations, given that they can be the first factors that impact interest in a card. So along those lines, let’s take a look at those details for the Amex Blue Cash Preferred.

The Amex Blue Cash Preferred is currently offering the following welcome bonus: You may be eligible for as high as $300 cash back after spending $3,000 in purchases on your new Card in the first 6 months. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer. Cash back is received as Reward Dollars, redeemable for statement credit or for other select options. Terms Apply.

That’s a solid bonus for a card at this price point, and the six month window gives you plenty of time to hit the spending requirement. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

Amex cards tend to be fairly easy to get approved for if you have excellent credit. A few rules to know:

As you can see, this card is marketed as offering a bonus “as high as” a certain amount. The way this works, you can apply for the Amex Blue Cash Preferred Card, and then find out your offer amount. Then you can decide whether you want to accept the offer or not. That’s an unconventional approach for a welcome offer. At least Amex has the “apply with confidence” feature, so there won’t be a hard pull unless you accept the offer.

The Amex Blue Cash Preferred has a $0 intro annual fee for the first year, then $95. (Rates & Fees). That puts it in line with other mid-range cards. No first year annual fee is a nice perk, as it lets you test the card and see how much value you’re getting before you commit to the ongoing fee.

If you decide the card isn’t working for you after the first year, you can always downgrade to the no annual fee Blue Cash Everyday Card.

You can add authorized users to the card at no extra cost, so that their spending can help you rack up rewards.

I wouldn’t recommend using the Amex Blue Cash Preferred Card outside the U.S. or for purchases in foreign currencies. The 2.7% foreign transaction fee will eat into your rewards (Rates & Fees). There are plenty of other cards with no foreign transaction fees that are better suited for international spending.

The Amex Blue Cash Preferred has some excellent bonus categories, especially if you spend a lot at U.S. supermarkets and on streaming. Below is a full breakdown.

This is the headline feature of the Amex Blue Cash Preferred, and it’s the single best cash back rate for U.S. supermarket spending that I’m aware of. You earn 6% cash back at U.S. supermarkets on up to $6,000 per year in purchases (then 1%). This is the only bonus category with an earning cap.

To put that in perspective, if you spend $500 a month on U.S. supermarket spending, you’d earn $360 per year in cash back from this category alone. That more than covers the $95 annual fee.

Note that supermarkets don’t include superstores, warehouse clubs (like Costco or Sam’s Club), or discount stores. If most of your grocery shopping happens at a traditional supermarket, this card is incredibly rewarding.

The Amex Blue Cash Preferred also offers 6% cash back on select U.S. streaming subscriptions. The list of qualifying services is quite long and includes most of the major platforms: Netflix, Hulu, Disney+, ESPN+, HBO Max, Spotify, Apple TV, Apple Music, Amazon Music Unlimited, YouTube Premium, YouTube TV, Peacock, Sling TV, and many more.

If you’re spending $50 to $100 a month across streaming services (which many households are these days), that 6% adds up nicely.

The Amex Blue Cash Preferred offers 3% cash back on transit purchases, including taxis, ridesharing, parking, tolls, trains, and buses. If you commute by public transit or use rideshare services regularly, this is a solid bonus category.

With the Amex Blue Cash Preferred, you also earn 3% cash back at eligible U.S. gas stations, with no caps. Note that this doesn’t include gas purchased at superstores, supermarkets, or warehouse clubs that sell fuel.

For purchases that don’t fall into the bonus categories, you earn 1% cash back. This is the one weak spot of the card. At just 1% on non-bonused spending, you’ll want to pair this card with something that earns a better return on everyday purchases (more on that below).

With the Amex Blue Cash Preferred, you earn Reward Dollars that can be redeemed as statement credits, and there’s no minimum cash back balance required before you can redeem. It’s simple and straightforward, though it’s worth knowing that you can’t use cash back to pay your minimum payment due.

As is the case for any credit card, it’s also important to consider the benefits and credits offered, if any. The Amex Blue Cash Preferred has a reasonable annual fee, so what are the benefits like? Well, they’re potentially pretty solid, and can help justify the annual fee…

The Amex Blue Cash Preferred offers up to $10 back per month ($120 per year) as a statement credit when you use your enrolled card to purchase a subscription, including a bundle subscription, on DisneyPlus.com, Hulu.com, or Stream.ESPN.com U.S. websites, with no minimum purchase requirement. Subscription is subject to auto-renewal. (Enrollment required)

Another Amex Blue Cash Preferred benefit is access to Amex Presale Tickets® and Amex Reserved Tickets®, which can come in handy if you’re trying to score tickets to an in-demand concert or sporting event.

The Amex Blue Cash Preferred also includes an introductory 0% APR offer that can give you some breathing room on purchases and balance transfers.

Enjoy 0% intro APR on purchases and balance transfers for 12 months from the date of account opening. After that, your APR will be a variable APR of 19.74% - 28.74%

This could be helpful if you need to transfer an existing credit card balance and have some time to pay it off before interest kicks in, or if you need some extra time to pay off a big upcoming purchase. Just make sure you pay off your balance in full before the intro period ends, or you’ll be on the hook for interest after all.

One benefit that doesn’t get enough attention is the Amex Offers program. This gives you access to targeted deals with a variety of retailers, just by registering your card and making an eligible purchase.

Different Amex cards get different offers, so having multiple Amex cards in your wallet means more chances to save. Across my Amex cards, this program saves me hundreds of dollars per year.

The Amex Blue Cash Preferred Card has fewer travel protections than more premium Amex cards, but it does come with coverage to protect your rental car when you charge the rental to this card. The coverage applies for eligible damage or theft, and it’s secondary, so it kicks in after your own car insurance. There are some exclusions, and it doesn’t include liability coverage, so check your card benefits guide for the full details.

Car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc.

The Amex Blue Cash Preferred Card offers the following benefits when you shop with the card:

These are all helpful benefits that you hopefully won’t have to use (though they do provide some peace of mind). Just remember you need to purchase the relevant items with your card to get this coverage.

Purchase Protection is an embedded benefit of your Card Membership and requires no enrollment. It can help protect Covered Purchases made on your Eligible Card when they’re accidentally damaged, stolen, or lost, for up to 90 days from the Covered Purchase date. The coverage is limited to up to $10,000 per occurrence, up to $50,000 per Card Member account per calendar year. Coverage Limits Apply. Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. When an American Express® Card Member charges a Covered Purchase to an Eligible Card, Extended Warranty§ can provide up to one extra year added to the Original Manufacturer’s Warranty. Applies to warranties of five (5) years or less. Coverage is up to the actual amount charged to your Card for the item up to a maximum of $10,000; not to exceed $50,000 per Card Member account per calendar year. Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company.

I tend to lean toward points-earning cards for my own spending, but I totally get why a lot of people prefer cash back. It’s simple, flexible, and you can spend it however you want, including on travel. For that crowd, the Blue Cash Preferred is one of the best options out there.

If you’re someone who is looking to earn cash back and spends a lot at supermarkets, then the Amex Blue Cash Preferred Card is an exceptional choice, in my opinion — 6% cash back will add up quickly.

The 6% cash back on streaming, and 3% cash back on transit and gas stations, will add up quickly as well, and up to $120 Disney streaming credit could be worth more than the annual fee.

However, this isn’t the card I would be using for your everyday spending, as you’d only earn 1% cash back in the categories that aren’t eligible for bonuses. So I’d acquire this card specifically with the intent of using it in the categories offering bonuses.

So, let’s take a look at what other cards you should potentially be considering.

If you like the idea of an Amex cash back card but aren’t sure about paying an annual fee, the Blue Cash Everyday Card from American Express (learn more) is the no annual fee alternative where you can earn as high as $200 cash back after spending $2,000 in purchases on your new Card in the first six months. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer. Cash back is received as Reward Dollars, redeemable for statement credit or for other select options. Terms Apply.

Here’s how the two Blue Cash cards compare:

In my opinion, the Blue Cash Preferred is well worth the annual fee if you spend a meaningful amount at supermarkets. The jump from 3% to 6% on U.S. supermarkets adds up fast. If you spend $500 a month at supermarkets, that extra 3% earns you $180 more per year, which nearly doubles the annual fee.

The Blue Cash Everyday does have one unique advantage: 3% cash back on U.S. online retail purchases, which the Preferred doesn’t offer. If you do a lot of online shopping and less grocery shopping, the Everyday could actually come out ahead.

The good news is that you can always start with the Blue Cash Preferred and downgrade to the Blue Cash Everyday after the first year if the math doesn’t work out.

If you’re just looking for the simplest cash back credit card, it’s tough to go wrong with the Citi Double Cash® Card (learn more). The card offers 1% cash back when you make a purchase, and 1% cash back when you pay for that purchase, for a total of 2% back on every purchase. That’s a solid return on everyday spending, and you don’t have to keep track of any bonus spending categories.

If you’re deciding between the Blue Cash Preferred and a mid-range card from another issuer, the $95 annual fee Citi Strata Premier Card (learn more) is worth considering. These two cards serve pretty different purposes, but they’re at the same price point:

The Blue Cash Preferred wins on supermarkets and streaming, hands down. If those are your biggest spending categories, the Blue Cash Preferred is the better card.

The Strata Premier is the more well-rounded card overall. It earns 3x points across five major categories (dining, gas, supermarkets, airfare, hotels), has no foreign transaction fees, and its ThankYou points can be transferred to airline and hotel partners for potentially much more than face value. If you travel or eat out a lot, the Strata Premier likely comes out ahead.

One final card worth considering alongside the Blue Cash Preferred Card is the American Express® Gold Card (learn more). It has a significantly higher annual fee, but it’s unbeatable for earning rewards at U.S. supermarkets — you’ll earn transferable Membership Rewards points too, rather than cash back.

The Blue Cash Preferred is the best cash back card for supermarket spending, and it’s not particularly close. If groceries and streaming are a big part of your monthly budget, this card can deliver serious returns, especially with the 6% rate on both categories plus the Disney streaming credit.

The annual fee pays for itself quickly if you’re spending even a moderate amount at supermarkets. Pair it with a card like the Citi Double Cash for your non-bonused spending, and you’ve got a strong cash back setup.

Just keep in mind that the 1% rate on everyday purchases means this card works best as a specialist, not your only card. Use it where it shines, and let a flat-rate card handle the rest.

If you want to learn more about the Blue Cash Preferred Card or want to apply, follow this link.

The following links will direct you to the rates and fees for mentioned American Express Cards. These include: Blue Cash Everyday® Card from American Express (Rates & Fees), and Blue Cash Preferred® Card from American Express (Rates & Fees).

#6169. Trump Says His Private Pilot Used To Use Foreign Air Traffic Control Because The American System Is So Bad

Donald Trump says his private pilot used another country’s air traffic control because the American system was so bad. He wouldn’t identify the country, as though his pilot had discovered a better provider for approaches into Teterboro and didn’t want everyone else signing up. Pilots don’t get that choice. And this isn’t just an ambiguous reference to flying overseas. Trump has made this claim before and described landing in New York, Florida and Tennessee. At his Friday press conference, Trump said his “pilot would use the air traffic control from a totally different country.” This was supposedly before his first term, 11 or 12 years ago. Then he declared, “I know a lot about air traffic control.” Watch Trump describe his pilot using another country’s air traffic control — Aaron Rupar (@atrupar), November 20, 2026 Air traffic control assigns clearances and separates aircraft sharing the same airspace. The controller responsible for your flight changes as you move between sectors and facilities. Your pilot can request a different route or altitude. They can reject an unsafe instruction. They can’t decide to use a different country’s air traffic control service because they like it better. And there’s a clear division of responsibilities. Pilots fly the aircraft and request changes to clearances when needed. Controllers coordinate the traffic. Could There Be A Real Story Behind This? I’ve tried to come up with something plausible, to create the most generous interpretation of these remarks. The best I can do is that Trump is confusing navigation equipment with air traffic control. Perhaps his pilot told him about a preferred navigation system, approach procedure or a piece of equipment he liked from overseas, and that became a story about choosing another country’s controllers. There are also real circumstances where an American flight uses foreign air traffic services: Crossing the North Atlantic. A flight to Scotland could pass through airspace handled by Nav Canada’s Gander operation and Britain’s Shanwick operation. Taking a route through Canada. A pilot could request a route that avoids congested U.S. sectors and spends more time in Canadian airspace (but it doesn’t give Canadian controllers responsibility for a landing in Tennessee). Flying in U.S. airspace assigned to Canadian controllers. “American airspace means American controllers” isn’t always true. Under a 1963 agreement, the United States delegates control of certain portions of its airspace within 50 nautical miles of the Canadian border. But the government assigned that responsibility, the pilot doesn’t choose their preferred controller. None of this would reconcile his comments with what he claimed on May 8, 2025. So, if I’m landing in New York or Florida or Tennessee, they’re using a system from another country. He repeated the story on June 27, 2025, too. So this is a recurring explanation of how he thinks flying works. The U.S. System Really Does Need Fixing I’ve been writing about the FAA’s antiquated technology and failed modernization efforts for years. Last week’s nationwide ground stop followed a contractor’s router installation that disrupted communications and radar information across much of the country. I’ve also pushed back when Trump claimed credit for the 2017 aviation safety record, when he blamed diversity hiring after the Washington crash without evidence, and when he suggested departing air traffic controllers could be quickly replaced. Training qualified controllers takes years. In fact, I supported the direction of Trump’s 2017 air traffic control proposal. He wanted to move operations into a separate nonprofit, with the FAA retaining safety regulation. A Canadian-style organization could finance upgrades without depending on annual congressional appropriations, and the FAA would stop regulating its own service. This year I challenged FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford’s attempt to rewrite that history as though airlines had hijacked Trump’s modernization plan and turned it into a debate over spinning off the system. Trump had announced the separate nonprofit himself. Maybe he think it actually existed, before he was President. I’ve been writing about the FAA’s antiquated technology and failed modernization efforts for years. Last week’s nationwide ground stop followed a contractor’s router installation that disrupted communications and radar information across much of the country.

I’ve also pushed back when Trump claimed credit for the 2017 aviation safety record, when he blamed diversity hiring after the Washington crash without evidence, and when he suggested departing air traffic controllers could be quickly replaced. Training qualified controllers takes years.

In fact, I supported the direction of Trump’s 2017 air traffic control proposal. He wanted to move operations into a separate nonprofit, with the FAA retaining safety regulation. A Canadian-style organization could finance upgrades without depending on annual congressional appropriations, and the FAA would stop regulating its own service.

This year I challenged FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford’s attempt to rewrite that history as though airlines had hijacked Trump’s modernization plan and turned it into a debate over spinning off the system. Trump had announced the separate nonprofit himself. Maybe he think it actually existed, before he was President.

#6168. American & Israir Partner On US-Israel Flights: Logical, But Limited

American Airlines and Israir Airlines have just announced plans to partner for flights between the United States and Israel. For now don’t expect huge implications, but over time, this has the potential to evolve.

American and Israir are launching a commercial partnership focused on enhanced travel options between Israel and the United States. The partnership is expected to expand in phases, delivering some benefits to customers. American plans to resume flights to Tel Aviv (TLV) as of late March 2027.

How is this partnership expected to play out?

For context, as of March 27, 2027, American plans to resume flights between New York and Tel Aviv, using the Boeing 777-200ER. Israir operates five weekly flights between Tel Aviv and New York, using an Airbus A330-200 (funny enough, the airline flies ex-American A330s, which the airline retired shortly after the start of the pandemic).

For those curious about the interiors of Israir’s A330s, below is a video of them (sorry, I don’t know what’s going on in the video, but I haven’t otherwise been able to find a cabin video).

Here’s how American’s SVP of Alliances, Anmol Bhargava, describes this:

“American looks forward to building a relationship with Israir that will give customers the convenient, well-connected travel options they desire. As we prepare to resume service between New York and Tel Aviv next spring, this partnership will help us deliver a stronger customer proposition in the market and create more opportunities for Israir’s travelers to connect beyond our JFK gateway.”

The dynamics of this partnership are interesting. There are a few things to keep in mind:

When it comes to the new partnership between American and Israir, here’s what’s I find noteworthy:

All-in-all, this is a pretty casual partnership. There’s no real downside here for American, since the carrier might just pick up a little bit of revenue on connecting Israir passengers beyond New York. Meanwhile Israir has a better framework for selling tickets beyond New York, which helps the carrier expand its potential customer base. But it is interesting how the codeshare is one-sided for now…

American Airlines and Israir Airlines are launching a partnership for flights between the United States and Israel. Israir will be codesharing on American’s flight between New York and Tel Aviv (when that resumes in late March 2027, in theory), while American will have an interline agreement with Israir, allowing Israir passengers to connect on American flights beyond New York.

We may see a closer level of cooperation between the two airlines in the future, including possible AAdvantage perks, but nothing has been finalized there yet. I wouldn’t read too much into this partnership for now, and think it falls more in the category of “better than nothing,” rather than anything beyond that.

What do you make of the new partnership between American and Israir?

#6166. Mexico’s President Spent 21 Hours In Coach Getting To China—And Sat In A Middle Seat

Mexico’s President Claudia Sheinbaum spent about 21 hours getting to China in economy on China Southern Airlines. She reportedly sat in 33B. A middle seat, on a trip across the Pacific, to represent her country at a summit of world leaders. That’s quite a contrast with Donald Trump’s enthusiasm for accepting a Boeing 747 in royal configuration from Qatar. But while Sheinbaum is winning praise for saving taxpayers money, she should have flown business class. The 64 year old president traveled from Mexico City through Tijuana to Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. Here’s her departure update: Claudia Sheinbaum’s update on her trip to Shenzhen, November 15, 2026 21 Hours Includes The Stop In Tijuana She left Mexico City early Sunday, November 15, on China Southern flight CZ8032 and arrived in Shenzhen on Monday. The Airbus A350-900 made its scheduled technical stop in Tijuana along the way. The first flight took 3 hours 12 minutes and the transpacific segment clocked in at 14 hours 56 minutes, with about two and a half hours on the ground between them. China Southern operates the route nonstop from Shenzhen to Mexico City, with the Tijuana stop in the other direction. Several stories report that seat 33B is in the back of the aircraft. In fact, it’s the front of standard economy. On arrival she posted video of her welcome in Shenzhen. An airport bus brought her to the red carpet, where an honor guard and performers waited. She received a presidential welcome. Which reminds me a little bit of when I’ve booked first class awards on Lufthansa, but the intra-European segment was only available in coach. Nobody ever could quite figure out how a coach passenger had a vehicle waiting for them on the tarmac. She returned on China Southern flight CZ8031 and shared a photo with the crew: Claudia Sheinbaum thanks the crew of flight CZ8031 on her return from Shenzhen Mexico Sold Its Presidential 787 Sheinbaum is continuing a practice established by Andrés Manuel López Obrador. In July 2020, I wrote about Mexico’s president flying Delta coach and connecting in Atlanta to meet Trump. He had an exit row aisle seat on a Delta flight from Mexico City. Delta was blocking middle seats at the time, too, due to the pandemic. Reforma’s video of López Obrador boarding Delta for his Washington trip, July 7, 2020 López Obrador refused to use Mexico’s presidential Boeing 787-8. After years of trying to find a buyer, Mexico sold it to Tajikistan for about $92 million in 2023. He said the proceeds would fund two hospitals. This isn’t Sheinbaum’s first long trip in coach, either. In April I covered her economy trip to Europe, flying through Madrid to Barcelona and returning to Mexico City on Aeromexico. She posted a photo of herself working at her coach seat: Claudia Sheinbaum working during her April 2026 trip to Barcelona I thought that was performative then. A president’s time has value, and so does being rested for the work the country is sending her to do. Aeromexico business class would have provided better rest and opportunity to work. Pringles, Princes, And A Qatari 747 I’ve covered plenty of politicians and royals flying coach. Prince William flew American Airlines economy from Memphis to Dallas in 2014, in a bulkhead window seat on an Airbus A319. He’s also flown Ryanair and taken the family on Flybe, carrying their hand luggage. Prince Harry and Meghan Markle flew British Airways coach to Nice for New Year’s in 2017. They and three bodyguards occupied the last three rows, with empty seats around them. T Argentina’s Javier Milei flew coach on his trip to Davos in January 2024. Given Argentina’s finances and the spending cuts he wanted the public to accept, there was a political purpose for the symbolism. David Cameron was photographed eating Pringles and working on his iPad aboard easyJet in 2015, while traveling to Portugal. I liked that one. William and Harry’s grandfather Prince Philip, though, described the improvements in air travel over his lifetime with the qualification, “provided you don’t travel in something called economy class, which sounds ghastly.” Meanwhile, thhe Pentagon accepted Qatar’s Boeing 747-8 in May 2025 for Trump’s use as Air Force One. It was widely described as a $400 million gift. I covered the Qatari jet’s conversion this summer, including the decision to preserve its luxury interior and the plan for it eventually to go to Trump’s presidential library. The U.S. president needs secure communications, protection, and the ability to keep working while traveling. That can justify dedicated aircraft. Sheinbaum’s coach trip earned publicity, including favorable attention in China while she was there to meet its leaders. But saving the difference between coach and business class is simply a poor value tradeoff when the cost is productive time and sleep for someone with a high opportunity cost. #6164. Britt bill would launch national office to combat financial fraud

Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

A bill introduced by Sen. Katie Britt on Wednesday aims to combat a rising diversity of financial fraud by unifying the U.S. effort to fight it.

The draft bill would establish a National Office for Scam and Fraud Prevention in the White House that would coordinate federal, state and private sector efforts. It is aimed at ensuring that federal agencies, law enforcement, financial institutions, telecommunications and technology companies and other groups work together, according to an overview from Britt.

The new office would promote intelligence sharing across the public and private sectors, coordinate consumer education efforts and improve assistance for victims.

Britt, R-Ala., said the effort is needed because fraudsters operate nimbly utilizing social media while taking advantage of fragmented or disorganized responses from individual companies and government agencies.

“This effort is about bringing everyone to the table and making sure our response keeps pace with the criminals who are exploiting new technologies and gaps between sectors,” she said in a statement. “When we work together to identify threats earlier and share information more effectively, we can better protect American families and businesses.”

The office would develop a “lexicon of fraud” so that terms for different kinds of scams are standardized between various federal law enforcement agencies to promote a “whole-of-government response,” a Britt aide said.

The office also would work to broaden the approach to combating fraud beyond just having financial institutions reimburse victims. It would tap telecommunications and technology companies to address fraud at its source, such as rip-offs that start as text messages, social media posts or online advertisements.

Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. She is the sponsor of a bill that would allow state, local and tribal law enforcement agencies to use federal grant funding to investigate financial fraud, particularly scams targeted at the elderly.

The measure highlights the prevalence of "pig butchering," a common technique where a predator cultivates a personal relationship with a victim over many months to extract the most cash.

The House passed its version of the bill in September with overwhelming bipartisan support. The House sponsor is Rep. Zach Nunn, R-Iowa.

Senior financial abuse also was the focus of a bill the House passed in an overwhelming 414-2 vote in June. The legislation, sponsored by Rep. Ann Wagner, R-Mo., would codify Securities and Exchange Commission guidance that permits mutual funds and their agents to postpone the sale of securities if there is a reasonable belief that financial exploitation of someone who is elderly or disabled is occurring

It's not clear whether the Senate will take action on these bills or Britt's by the end of the year.

“If it doesn’t get through in the lame duck, it will continue to be a priority in the 120th [Congress],” the Britt aide said.

#6163. JSX Buys New Pacific Airlines—42 Seat Jets Could Bring Its Private Terminal Flights To More Travelers

JSX has acquired New Pacific Airlines, and plans to bring the failed airline back with 42 seat Embraer regional jets. That’s 12 more seats than JSX sells on its planes today, and it gives them a way to grow beyond the limits of their current operation. I think this fits a company that’s been unusually creative about finding markets and figuring out how to serve them. They brought turboprops to Santa Monica’s shortened runway and used a free membership program to gain access to Teterboro in order to serve New York. JSX isn’t laying out the New Pacific strategy yet. Asked about the deal, they tell me: JSX is continually evaluating opportunities to support its long-term growth and bring its distinctive flying experience to more Customers and more communities. As part of that work, we are pursuing additional pathways that could provide even more ways to deliver our award-winning service in the future. Our focus remains on the exceptional experience, convenience, and hospitality our Customers have come to expect from JSX. New Pacific has filed its intent to resume flying and requested a waiver of the usual 45 day advance filing requirement. An operating projection calls for: Embraer ERJ145-LR aircraft with 42 seats. Two aircraft initially, growing to six by the fifth month. 10,106 flights and roughly 309,000 passenger boardings in the first year. Flights averaging about 1.2 hours gate to gate, with staffing growing to 104 employees. New Pacific used to be Northern Pacific, the startup that wanted to connect the mainland U.S. and Asia through Anchorage using Boeing 757s. It seemed unlikely to work anyway but the closure of Russian airspace to U.S. carriers kept them from even trying. It pivoted to short domestic routes and then sports and corporate charters. I reported its shutdown last November, just two weeks after it announced an all-business class venture with beOnd. The bankruptcy process disposed of its 757s. What it has instead is Part 121 certification allowing operations beyond the 30 passenger limit of JSX’s current Part 135 public charter model. I first flew JSX home from Southwest Airlines Media Day in late 2022. JSX’s 4 p.m. departure got me home for dinner, an hour ahead of the Southwest flight I would have taken. I reached the terminal 19 minutes before departure. In Austin, I was in a Lyft less than ten minutes after touchdown. The plane was comfortable, with a seat on each side of the aisle and a side table next to mine. But getting my time back was what made it worth paying more (but honestly, not much more). I didn’t need a bigger airport lounge. I needed to spend less time at the airport. By my March 2023 visit to JSX’s headquarters, they’d fixed my one real complaint: no internet. JSX was the first carrier with Starlink, and the first to finish equipping its full fleet. Notably United Airlines owns a stake in JSX. The early JSX adoption is likely related to United’s head start with Starlink among major airlines. JSX’s business depended on putting several things together: inexpensive used aircraft, a comfortable cabin, friendly service and airports that let customers avoid wasting time. At the time, airport real estate was their biggest constraint. Finding another city with people willing to buy a ticket wasn’t enough. They needed somewhere to put the operation. Look at Santa Monica. The city is literally closing the airport and shortened its runway to 3,500 feet. JSX brought in ATR 42-600 turboprops configured with 30 seats. They found an aircraft suited to an airport that’s convenient for customers on the west side of Los Angeles, and obtained permission to operate despite the local politics. At Teterboro, the solution involved how they sold tickets. The airport prohibits publicly advertised scheduled passenger service. JSX put the flights behind a Club JSX login, limited bookings to members, and marketed the destination publicly as New York City. Joining the program is free, but joining is how they gain access to the airport. Those are different solutions to different problems. With New Pacific, JSX gains the ability to operate with more than 30 seats. My guess is that they see markets where a different version of their product could work, with more passengers sharing the cost of each departure. There is a regulatory insurance benefit. American Airlines, Southwest and the big pilots union have pushed to restrict JSX’s business model. I anticipated that sort of campaign in my first review. Having a Part 121 operation would be useful if the rules change. But the Federal Aviation Administration’s current agenda lists its public charter rulemaking as a long-term action with the next step undetermined. They never closed the rulemaking effort. But I think it’s possible to overread the regulatory risk insurance strategy here. They could still use private terminals with a part 121 operation and 42 seats. Federal security rules provide for scheduled and public charter flights with 31 to 60 seats outside the usual secure terminal area. This wouldn’t work at every airport JSX currently serves due to airport certification requirements. And part 121 means different pilot requirements, including mandatory age 65 retirement (they couldn’t use their ex-American and Southwest senior captains). If they do plan 42 seats that a different product – still more generous than a 50-seat sardine can but not nearly as spacious as the current 30-seat setup JSX appears to have a plan to add 40% more seats to some of the regional jets they own, and operate them under a scheduled airline. They haven’t said what they’re actually planning, but it may be a different niche than their current model rather than the assumed ‘buy a scheduled airline in case the next administration capitulates to lobbyists and puts them out of business’ the way ALPA, Southwest and American sought to do under the last administration. I think this fits a company that’s been unusually creative about finding markets and figuring out how to serve them. They brought turboprops to Santa Monica’s shortened runway and used a free membership program to gain access to Teterboro in order to serve New York. JSX isn’t laying out the New Pacific strategy yet. Asked about the deal, they tell me:

JSX is continually evaluating opportunities to support its long-term growth and bring its distinctive flying experience to more Customers and more communities. As part of that work, we are pursuing additional pathways that could provide even more ways to deliver our award-winning service in the future. Our focus remains on the exceptional experience, convenience, and hospitality our Customers have come to expect from JSX.

New Pacific has filed its intent to resume flying and requested a waiver of the usual 45 day advance filing requirement. An operating projection calls for:

New Pacific used to be Northern Pacific, the startup that wanted to connect the mainland U.S. and Asia through Anchorage using Boeing 757s. It seemed unlikely to work anyway but the closure of Russian airspace to U.S. carriers kept them from even trying. It pivoted to short domestic routes and then sports and corporate charters. I reported its shutdown last November, just two weeks after it announced an all-business class venture with beOnd.

The bankruptcy process disposed of its 757s. What it has instead is Part 121 certification allowing operations beyond the 30 passenger limit of JSX’s current Part 135 public charter model.

I first flew JSX home from Southwest Airlines Media Day in late 2022. JSX’s 4 p.m. departure got me home for dinner, an hour ahead of the Southwest flight I would have taken. I reached the terminal 19 minutes before departure. In Austin, I was in a Lyft less than ten minutes after touchdown.

The plane was comfortable, with a seat on each side of the aisle and a side table next to mine. But getting my time back was what made it worth paying more (but honestly, not much more). I didn’t need a bigger airport lounge. I needed to spend less time at the airport.

By my March 2023 visit to JSX’s headquarters, they’d fixed my one real complaint: no internet. JSX was the first carrier with Starlink, and the first to finish equipping its full fleet. Notably United Airlines owns a stake in JSX. The early JSX adoption is likely related to United’s head start with Starlink among major airlines.

JSX’s business depended on putting several things together: inexpensive used aircraft, a comfortable cabin, friendly service and airports that let customers avoid wasting time. At the time, airport real estate was their biggest constraint. Finding another city with people willing to buy a ticket wasn’t enough. They needed somewhere to put the operation.

#6162. Wry and Wistful Landscapes at Kansas City’s Splendid Nelson-Atkins Museum

The museum needs to ditch its proposed expansion, an unneeded temple to therapy culture.

Joel Sternfeld, McLean, Virginia, December 4, 1978, printed 2005, dye transfer print.

The Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art, © Joel Sternfeld

‘E verything’s Up to Date in Kansas City” — that few minutes of pure effervescence in Oklahoma refers to Kansas City circa 1907, when it was in the middle of its version of the City Beautiful movement. New boulevards, new, fancy neighborhoods, hundreds of fountains, and much more were in the works. The sparkle of a new art museum was in the civic eye, too. The Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art didn’t open its doors until 1933, but better late than never. It’s an essential visit for art lovers.

I visited last month and saw the very enjoyable exhibition American Prospects and Landscape Photography, 1839 to Today. It presents Joel Sternfeld’s lovely, often sad, wry, late-1970s and early-1980s landscape photographs in the context of the American landscape-photography genre. I love Sternfeld’s work. Born in 1944, he was the cutting-edge photographer who took color landscape photography mainstream, mostly through American Prospects, his portfolio of photographs published in book form in 1987. Color? Cutting-edge in the ’80s? Well, 1987 is about to be 40 years ago, so it qualifies as days of yore, and what has became American Prospects started in the late ’70s, when Sternfeld started an epic road trip to make art about Americans and the land. Landscape photography was, à la Ansel Adams, commonly in black and white, thought to evoke grandeur and mystery. What pushed Sternfeld to color was the advent of Kodak Vericolor III film in the 1970s. It delivered accurate, vibrant color and was good for various lighting and especially skin tones.

Brian T. Allen is National Review’s art critic.

On “Wry and Wistful Landscapes at Kansas City’s Splendid Nelson-Atkins Museum”

The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop after telecommunications problems affected air traffic control centers. Then on Monday, a software bug at JPMorgan Chase slowed transactions for hours, and customers of at least five other banks reported problems too. The same day, United Airlines delayed hundreds of flights over a problem with the system that calculates a plane’s weight before takeoff. Five very different events raised the same question: What happens when the thing you count on is suddenly unavailable?

#6160. United Nigeria Airlines Flew Passengers To The Wrong City—3 Years Later, Chairman Admits They Lied About It

United Nigeria Airlines flew passengers to the wrong city and blamed the weather. Three years later, they’re admitting it was all a lie. I covered this incident on November 28, 2023, including the conflict between the pilot reportedly acknowledging a wrong flight plan and the airline insisting on a weather diversion. Now, Live and Let’s Fly flags the airline chairman’s admission that the passengers’ explanation was right. Executive Chairman Obiora Okonkwo revisited the episode at the World Public Relations Forum in Abuja on November 17. A dispatcher had entered the wrong destination in the paperwork. The pilots flew there. The flight attendants apparently believed they’d reached the city everyone bought tickets to. He described the weather explanation as “just a lie” and offered this advice: “The best way of public relations is to tell the truth, but tell it responsibly.” Passengers Were Welcomed To Abuja While Sitting In Asaba On November 26, 2023, flight 0504 left Lagos with passengers booked to Abuja, Nigeria’s capital. It landed in Asaba instead, about 200 miles away. This was United Nigeria Airlines, not United Airlines. Passengers reported that the flight attendants welcomed everyone to Abuja but then everyone discovered where they actually were. November 26, 2023 — Peacock (@dawisu) Another passenger shared video: We legit got scared sha. Laff wan kee me 😅 pic.twitter.com/sWxbnJeDna— Lord Macky (@AugustineMacky) November 26, 2023 The airline’s original statement blamed “poor destination weather”, said the pilot knew about the diversion, and attributed the confusion to an incorrect cabin announcement. The plane eventually continued to Abuja. The Investigation Uncovered The Truth The flight used an Airbus A320 operated by Bulgaria’s Fly2Sky for United Nigeria Airlines. Fly2Sky said at the time that United Nigeria had assigned it a Lagos–Asaba flight the previous day and hadn’t requested a change during the pilots’ preflight briefing. The Nigerian regulator identified failures well beyond one person entering a destination incorrectly. In its findings there was: Poor coordination between United Nigeria’s operations center and the company supplying the aircraft. No joint preflight briefing between the pilots and flight attendants. United Nigeria’s failure to monitor the leased aircraft through its operations center. Failure to follow the approved flight plan filed with air traffic control. The chairman story is about a dispatch error. The regulator, though, laid out several opportunities to prevent it. British Airways Has Done It, Too In March 2019, a British Airways flight scheduled from London City to Düsseldorf went to Edinburgh after the pilots received paperwork for the wrong destination. The passengers had bought a flight to Germany but the flight took them to Scotland. A few weeks later, Scandinavian Airlines sent a Copenhagen–Florence flight to Bologna. That was a deliberate decision made before departure because the pilots lacked the correct routing information for Florence. They flew to Bologna with plans to bus passengers onward. It’s just that they kept this information to themselves. And in August 2025, I covered AirAsia X passengers being welcomed to Incheon after their Kuala Lumpur flight landed at Seoul’s Gimpo airport, about 20 miles away. Here’s the Instagram video from that coverage: View the video shared by @rizalhakimm_punyer on Instagram AirAsia X said it had intentionally diverted for fuel because bad weather had caused congestion at Incheon. It acknowledged an incorrect cabin announcement, said the captain corrected it, and offered travel vouchers. Okonkwo also used his conference appearance to discuss a passenger upset that an advertised 11:30 a.m. flight had left at 11:20. He said he’d initially wanted to shout back, but instead responded, “I apologise for United Nigeria Airline leaving on time.” An airline chairman giving a speech about accurately convey what on-time means. #6159. Democrats nominate Jeffries to be House speaker, a historic first

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., flanked by House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., and House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., hold a press conference in the Capitol after the House Democratic leadership elections on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries won a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday setting him up to be the nation’s first Black speaker of the House, a historic step that follows Democrats’ staggering election wins earlier this month.

Jeffries, who had called for a recorded vote of the more than 250-member caucus that will serve in the next Congress despite facing no announced opponent, won decisively, 251-11. The margin suggests Jeffries will easily surpass the necessary 218 votes he will need on the House floor when the full chamber votes in January.

“It's a high honor and a distinct privilege to stand before the American people today as a Democratic nominee to be the next Speaker of the United States House of Representatives,” Jeffries said at a press conference following the election.

While Jeffries celebrates his win, he has continued to put an emphasis on unity before he faces what has been deemed the toughest job in Washington. Democrats’ massive majority will give him some margin for maneuvering as he balances the priorities of a complex caucus ranging from moderates to progressives.

“Our job is to fight MAGA extremism, not each other,” Jeffries responded when asked about the 11 defections and what they mean for the next Congress. “Fight MAGA extremism, and to get big things done for the American people, and that is what we are going to accomplish together, beginning on January 3rd.”

Seven of the 11 members who intended to vote against Jeffries released a statement saying that conversations with leadership are still “ongoing” and that there is “work to be done,” but noting there has been “meaningful progress.” The seven included Reps.- elect Darializa Avilia Chavelier, D-N.Y., Adam Hamawy, D-N.J., Frederick Haynes, D-Texas, Melat Kiros, D-Colo., Donovan McKinney, D-Mich., Chris Rabb, D-Pa., and Claire Valdez, D-N.Y.

“Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues,” they wrote. “We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations.”

Newly elected House Democrats will meet with former President Barack Obama Wednesday night, where party unity will also be a likely topic.

“This is the beginning of a new bargain, a new politics where hard work is honored and where people's voice is paramount, and where we have more confidence in the future than nostalgia for the past,” House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., said at the press conference.

Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., who made history two decades ago as the nation’s first female speaker, arrived for the vote chanting “Hakeem Jeffries!”, reflecting party leaders’ desire to start the long morning of balloting on a positive note.

Jeffries' nomination followed the election of current Democratic Caucus Vice Chairman Ted Lieu, D-Calif., to serve as the caucus chair in the next Congress. Separate votes followed Wednesday morning, keeping Jeffries' leadership team intact: Clark, as the new majority leader and Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., as majority whip.

At his news conference, Jeffries noted that Clark was also making history as the first woman ever to serve in the position. Aguilar will also be the first Latino to serve as majority whip.

“We've been looking at people's talents, not a particular gender or race, and I think that's a good thing,” outgoing Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, D-Md., a former majority leader, told reporters ahead of the election.

“I think Hakeem Jeffries is going to be a good speaker,” Hoyer continued. “He has the confidence of the caucus, and he has a good leadership team that is close knit and very organized.”

Jeffries expressed confidence in the weeks leading up to his securing the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who had said they remained “undecided” ahead of the election.

Pelosi was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to move forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

The entire leadership team will be tested despite their numerical advantage over Republicans by the same internal tensions facing Senate Democrats, where current Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., is being challenged for leadership of the majority by Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md.

Jeffries said Tuesday that the approach to the caucus vote mirrored the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who was best positioned to lead based on their “track record, experience and vision.”

Jeffries has already outlined some of his top priorities of his speakership such as a hefty healthcare agenda, immigration legislation, and a multitude of investigations into the Trump administration.

He also signaled Wednesday another area where his party’s restive base is likely to close ranks: oversight.

“House Democrats will hold the crooks accountable, not for partisan reasons, but for patriotic ones,” he said at his news conference.

#6158. Who Are the Republican Gatekeepers?

MAGA saw Russell Brand’s con job but welcomed him anyway.

Russell Brand arrives at Southwark Crown Court during the fourth week of his trial on charges of rape and sexual assault, in London, England, November 3, 2026.

#6157. These 14 apps and websites make award redemptions easier to find

Learn how to get started earning and redeeming rewards so you can make the most of your everyday spending.

See how far your points, miles and dollars go in TPG's first loyalty report.

See how TPG ranks the top US airlines for 2026.

As a senior writer for TPG, Tarah Chieffi helps readers travel better, more often and within their budget.

Mackenzie Roche is an editor on TPG’s content operations team. She previously worked for three years as a travel editor at U.S. News & World Report.

By commenting, you agree to our Community Guidelines to help create a positive space for conversation. The responses below are not provided or commissioned by the bank advertiser, our partners, or The Points Guy (“TPG”). They have not been reviewed, approved, or otherwise endorsed by any of these parties. All responses are submitted by individual contributors, and neither the bank advertiser, our partners, nor TPG are responsible for ensuring that all posts and/or questions are answered.... Read more

The Points Guy believes that credit cards can transform lives, helping you leverage everyday spending for cash back or travel experiences that might otherwise be out of reach. We publish editorial content and card reviews to help you find a great card to turn your goals into reality.

We may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened with our partners. This may impact how or where products appear.
